speakerposition: topic
Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire, with
the consent of the House if necessary, to move the following resolution:
That a Special Committee he appointed to consider questions relating to the pensions.

insurance and re-establishment of returned soldiers, and any amendments to the existing laws in relation thereto which may be proposed or considered necessary by the committee ; with power to send for persons, papers and records, to print from day to day its proceedings and the evidence taken, for the use of the committee, and to report from time to time; and that Rule 11 be suspended in relation thereto.
The House will remember that for at least two sessions a Special Committee has been appointed to deal with these matters, and, indeed, the administrative policy followed by this country, in relation to soldiers' re-establishment has been largely developed by these special committees. The returned men have on more than one occasion requested that a similar course be pursued this session. It may be the opinion of some hon. members that this subject has been already very thoroughly considered by Parliament, and that little, if anything, could be expected from another committee this session. Still, I believe it is the disposition of every hon. member, as I know it is the disposition of the Government, that the utmost pains be taken to see that nothing is left undone within the power of the country to take care of the just demands of those who did so much for us and for the world in the late war, and that to that end we should review all the administrative activities now under way looking to re-establishment, in order to ascertain the defects, if any exist-and there must be some-and to make recommendations as to what can be undertaken to improve upon our present methods; and generally to again go over the work done in previous sessions, so that we may all be sure that to the utmost of our power we are doing everything that can be done in the way of re-establishment.
I therefore have pleasure in moving this resolution which is virtually in the terms of similar motions adopted in previous sessions.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, as my name is mentioned as a member of this committee, I should like to make an inquiry with reference to it. The Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) has stated that requests have come to the Government from returned soldiers for the appointment of this committee. Have any particular requests been made by returned soldiers' organizations for the granting of bonuses or other privileges or rewards of a special character? As the Prime Minister has intimated, this subject was very thoroughly gone into in the three previous sessions, particularly in the last session, and a good deal of time-very properly so -has been given to the matter. Is it the intention of the Government that the work done last session shall be gone over during this session? Of course, it will depend in some degree on the committee itself. I should like to ask further whether the request for the appointment of the committee has been made by organizations of returned men, or only by private individuals.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad that the
hon. member (Mr. Beland) had brought up the several subjects dealt with in his remarks. I am not certain at the moment just what written requests the Government has for the appointment of this committee. In my travels through the country, though, it was the exception rather than otherwise that I should not be met at different cities, and met always by organized bodies of returned men, and the request proffered that this committee be re-appointed. I could name cities in which I recall being met by organized returned men representing not only the Great War Veterans' Association, but other organizations as well. I am quite free to state to the House that the Great War Veterans' Association, Federal Command, are very anxious for the re-appointment of this committee. They are, of course, one of the most numerous of all the soldier organizations.
I understand the hon. member also to ask what form of assistance Was generally

requested, and in that connection, what is expected to be done in relation to the bonus request. Well, many suggestions have been made, many requests have been urged, for all manner of things-improvements on present machinery, new schemes of assistance, such as loans for housing, and the like; I really would not be able to recite the number and variety of requests made. Certainly we have been asked to reconsider the Government's attitude in relation to a general bonus to returned men. I have invariably stated in answer to those requests that as respects that form of assistance, a general cash bonus to returned men, the Government had stated its policy adverse to the suggestion, and that that policy had not been changed.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The House resumed from Tuesday, March 8, the adjourned debate on the proposed resolution of Mr. Keefer, for the appointment of a Special Committee on deep water-
[Sir Henry Drayton.1
way transportation from the Great Lakes to the sea by way of the St. Lawrence river.
Mr. DANIEL D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):	Mr. Speaker,
subject of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) is not altogether new in this House, for we have discussed more than once most of what is included in that resolution. If the hon. gentleman will permit me, I should like to express my appreciation of his having brought this matter before the House and of the very able manner in which he presented his case. His arguments were strong, and I am sure that hon. members who had the opportunity of hearing his speech were pleased with his presentation of the case. But as he dealt with the subject matter of the resolution largely from the point of view of Ontario and the West, I think it is only fair that something should be said from the other end of the navigable route which he proposes to make a more complete avenue of trade than it is at present. In Nova Scotia we appreciate very highly inland navigation as far as it goes. The river St. Lawrence up as far as Montreal, and as much /further west as we can take full advantage of it, is pf great bene fit to the people of the province of Novr Scotia, and if this route is extended furthei west to Port Arthur, as the hon. membei proposes, it would certainly be much more beneficial to Nova Scotia and the Maritime Provinces generally than it is at present.
I need not remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the great opposition to Confederation in the Maritime Provinces, and particularly in Nova Scotia, was that by reason of the terms of Confederation, and the tariffs that were being imposed, our trade with the New England states was being shut off, and nothing appeared to be in sight to take its place. The people of the provinces of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and New Brunswick had at that time a very profitable trade with the New England states, and those who were opposed to Confederation contended, and with much force, that if this trade with the New England states was shut off by reason of Confederation, and no new trade routes opened in other directions, we would be getting the worst of the bargain. The building of the Intercolonial railway was therefore proposed as a remedy. We were told that it would afford an avenue for the sending of our goods to Ontario and western points. But I need not remind you. Sir, that we have

been very much disappointed in that respect. The freight rates have always been a hindrance to that trade, and now they are absolutely prohibitive. So far as our fish is concerned, I never heard of any of it being shipped west except one-half barrel of herring to Edmonton, and by the time it reached there, though its value was only $3, the freight had amounted to $8.50. That will show hon. gentlemen at once how impossible it is for us to hope for any trade with the West if we have no better means of transportation and no lower rates than the present railway communication affords. Let me say at once that I am for railways myself; if the rates were such that we could develop our trade by rail communication, I would be in favour of that means because with water transportation we are at best precluded at certain seasons of the year from the shipment of goods- traffic is suspended owing to the freezing over of the St. Lawrence. Canals are also frozen. So at certain seasons of the year there would always be a suspension of traffic owing to the waterway being unnavigable. That, of course, would not be the case with a railway; traffic would go on uninterruptedly. I need not say that in order to have a happy community and trade conditions that will be satisfactory to the different provinces, it is highly necessary that there should be reciprocity in trade between the several provinces. If we in the East get flour from Manitoba and the West, and manufactured goods from Ontario and Quebec, it is only rational to suppose that the people of the Maritime Provinces would be anxious to ship their goods west in exchange for the commodities that they buy there. If the traffic is all one way and our perishable goods cannot reach the people of the West in a fresh state, things will not be satisfactory. We therefore have a strong desire that there should be a means of getting our fish, and also our coal and lumber and whatever else we have to exchange, conveyed to the interior of the country in such a way that we shall be able to carry on a satisfactory trade.
Under present conditions it is highly desirable that we should encourage proper immigration to this country in order to swell our population. We have now only eight or eight and one-half millions of people, and we are faced with per capita responsibilities which are enormous, startling, to say the least; and it is not at all conducive to success in any attempt to bring immigrants to this or any other country when
you are obliged to tell them that the per capita debt is very large, the cost of living very high, and conditions such as to require a great deal of money to be able to live comfortably. If this navigation were opened it would have a tendency, for one thing, to cheapen food. We in the province-from which I come pay $16 per barrel for flour to-day, and have been paying in the neighbourhood of this sum for a number of years past. Perhaps it is a little cheaper now, but it is most extraordinary, Mr. Speaker, that in this country, where we have millions upon millions of bushels of wheat, and from year to year are told that there are large surpluses which we are not using, the poor miner, the poor lumberman, and the poor fisherman should have to pay $16 for a barrel of this staple commodity. There is something wrong somewhere when in this country, where we have such enormous production, and possibilities for further production of wheat, that we should have to pay as much for flour as in countries where wheat is not grown. I submit to the Government and to the people generally that there should be some way of surmounting this difficulty, and we should do everything in our power to bring about such a condition as would enable us with confidence to point out to prospective immigrants that at least one thing they might be certain of, and that was that there was plenty to eat for everybody in the country and that this was not an expensive place to live in. Now, if by opening of navigation between Port Arthur and the Atlantic -and I believe a great part has been opened already-we can make transportation cheaper, so that the flour from the West can reach the Maritime Provinces more easily than at present, our people would have every reason to anticipate great results.
So far as coal is concerned, let me say to the hon. gentleman who moved this resolution, and particularly to the Government, that one thing of which we can assure them is the fact that we have inexhaustible quantities of magnificent coal in the province of Nova Scotia. The people of Ontario have in the past been somewhat fastidious in regard to the quality of the coal they burn, and they have complained that our coal smoked, was sooty, and so forth. Well, let me say that we in Nova Scotia think we are just as good as any other people on earth,-not better, but just as good-and we find our coal quite satisfactory and conducive to comfort. It gives us all the warmth and comfort we need, and

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
for that reason we should have no hesitation whatever in recommending its use to the people of Ontario and other provinces further west to which it could be carried if this channel of communication were opened. As to the rohte which my hon. friend proposes. I am not in a position to offer very much criticism, but the sooner we get some satisfactory route the better.
The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) is not here, but I notice that the other night he made a speech on this question, and I wish to compliment him, in passing, on the adroitness which he displayed on that occasion. As a verbal juggler and acrobat I think he is unrivalled in this country of ours. People marvel at the dexterity of a man who is able to keep five or six balls in the air at the same time, but I never before saw a man who could keep five or six canals in the air with such success as the Minister of Railways and Canals. He did this with wonderful skill. By the way, I am glad to see that^ he has now come into the House, and I want to tell him that I should like to know how he was able to keep six canals in the air at once as he did the other day. I trust that he will be prevailed upon to do something besides dazzling the eyes of the Canadian people with this art of his of keeping these things in suspense. I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that in exchange for the things which the people of the West have to give us we can supply coal especially; and I think it is common knowledge also that we have inexhaustible schools of magnificent fish in Nova Scotia. It is unnecessary to tell hon. gentlemen in this House that fact, because, judging from the fish they eat in this part of the country, I would say that they know nothing whatever about good fish. This magnificent food they get only when it is spoiled. I have, been eating at the restaurant here since coming to Ottawa and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I never eat fish-I simply cannot; it is so unlike the genuine article that I cannot touch it. But as I see other gentleman eat it with apparent relish it strikes me that they do so because they do not know better. Now, if this navigation were opened and our ships could come up here with this article of food, I am sure that a great development would take place in connection with this industry, such as has never been known before. You know, Mr. Speaker, as well as I d6, that we are only touching the fringe of the industry. We are only at the edge of what can be produced from the fisheries in our prov-fMr. McKenzie.]
ince, and on the coast generally. I have no desire to take up more time. My heartiest approval is given to the resolution and the ideas which it contains. I again congratulate the hon. gentleman who introduced it upon bringing it before the House, and I sincerely trust that something substantial will result. The Minister of Railways and Canals made a speech the other night which I scarcely think the hon. mover might have expected as a comment on his resolution. We were told that a mere letter had been written to an official of this Government by the Minister of Railways telling him to do certain things. Well, suppose we had the answer which that official will make to the letter. What good is that? I am not aware of any arrangement between this country and the United States by which we can ask some official of this Government to make a certain report which could be binding Qn that country.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext:
Perhaps my hon.
friend will allow me to correct him. He does not understand what I really intended to convey with reference to the letter. I desired to explain to the House that the Government had taken action by writing a letter to the Chairman of the International Joint Waterways Commission bringing the matter to their attention, and also that an Order in Council had been passed bringing it before the United States Government. The whole question has been placed in the hands of the International Joint Waterways Commission-composed, of course, of representatives of both countries-and they are now making an examination and will present an official report. The report will be signed by the Commissioners of both countries, but, of course, it is not binding in any way. It will be merely an official report and both governments will be in a position to take action as they see fit.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I quite understood the position set forth by the minister the other night, and it is exactly as I stated. It was a letter written by the minister to an official of this Government. It was not a letter addressed to the Commission because I took particular care to find out what kind of a communication it was. If we expect to get a report from the Waterways Commission it would be in response to a request sent to it by this Government. The letter in question being merely a communication sent to one of our own officials that official would no doubt reply over his own signature, which would mean nothing

at all. Let me tell the Minister of Railways the matter is one that should be governed by common sense rules. In a matter of an international character it is customary for delegates appointed by this Government to meet delegates appointed by the Government of the United States; in other words this Government agrees with the Government of the United States, with the assistance of the Imperial Government, as to what things are to be done by the Waterways Commission. And when, following negotiations between the Governments concerned, an agreement is reached, then our Government will submit legislation to Parliament to confirm the agreement, and a similar course will be pursued by the United States in obtaining the sanction of Congress. Then it will be possible to make some progress with the question. But the mere sending of a letter by the Minister of Railways to an official of our own is certainly a capital way of delaying the matter and deferring action; no beneficial effect will follow as far as the country is concerned. I am sorry that in all the years this Government has been in power they have done nothing with this very important question, but merely cause one letter to be written to an official, good and capable as that official may be. Let me say to the Minister of Railways that I have the highest possible appreciation of his ability as a' politician; in fact there never was a better one connected with the Government. I hope the Government will hang on to him and that he will not be among those ministers whom it is intended to discard. As a man who will keep things going under the least possible pretext they will never get the like of him agaain. There is this further to be said about the present, Government :	They are so busy defending
their own heads, defending their lives and avoiding political graves and political graveyards, that they are paying very little attention to the business of the country; all their time and all their energy is devoted to keeping clear of the undertaker. Let me say in conclusion that I have much pleasure in assisting my good friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) in dealing with this very important question.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I am sorry I was not in the Chamber when this resolution was introduced. By reason of my absence all I have heard of the debate has been that portion of it which was contributed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) who has just resumed his seat. I have no desire to discuss the merits of the question, as to the desirability of constructing a deep waterway system between the Great Lakes and the Atlantic via the St. Lawrence route. As I understand it, the International Commission, on which the United States and Canada are equally represented, are thoroughly investigating whether the project is feasible from a commercial standpoint, and also whether it would reduce the cost of transportation. The International Commission, I believe, have been looking into the question very carefully and have been holding meetings not only in the various sections of Canada that might be interested in the scheme, but also at various points throughout the United States. If that is the case, and I have no doubt it is, the report of that commission, containing all the evidence given before it, will no doubt be available to every member of this House and each will then be able to consider the question from an intelligent standpoint.
The resolution itself asks that a committee of members of the House be appointed to re-investigate the very question that is being inquired into by the Deep Waterways Commission. Let me point out that it is absolutely impossible for a committee to sit, take evidence, and present a report without incurring a great deal of expense even if that committee be composed of members of Parliament. The resolution also asks that the committee be allowed to sit during the recess, which will also still further increase the expense. Now the estimates that have just been submitted to Parliament call for an expenditure of $586,000,000, and the Supplementary Estimates are yet to be presented. If that is not enough to stagger the mind of any hon. member and set him wondering where we are going to get our revenues, then he must be possessed of a very vivid imagination. Personally I am absolutely opposed to appointing unnecessary commissions of any kind, especially where it will simply be duplicating an enquiry already under way. Therefore, without discussing the matter further I wish to state that I am opposed to this resolution.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I
believe that the hon. gentleman who has just spoken is the only member who has said anything against the great nat-
4 p.m. ional and international undertaking contemplated by the resolu-

tion. I have closely watched the debate that has so far taken place, and there has been, with that exception, a unanimous expression of opinion in favour of this deep waterways canal and hydro-electric power development plan. Personally I believe it to be the most progressive step taken in Canada for many years. I regard this great waterway as a national asset, and the proposal to harness the forces of nature and place them at the service of mankind is one of its most desirable features. I agree with some hon. gentlemen that the estimate of the probable cost is doubtless far too small, but the territory to be benefited will be extremely large. The area of country which this great waterway will serve, not only in Canada but in the United States produces an abundance of agricultural products, oil, gas, and minerals of all kinds. I strongly believe in developing the St. Lawrence waterway system. In my opinion it will be a great adjunct to the Welland canal upon which so large an amount of money has already been expended. Let us remember that if we bring the channel up to the level of lake Ontario we have assured the wisdom of building the Welland canal.
Knowing something of hydro power development, I believe that the power which would be generated would of itself pay for the whole undertaking, as every horsepower that we did not need could be sold to the great New England centres at a handsome profit. This development, too, will also help us in the electrification of our railways, which is certain to come. Under the most scientific tests it has been demonstrated that the electrically driven locomotive is far and away superior to the steam locomotive both in tractive power and speed, to say nothing of ease of operation.
This country is exceedingly fortunate in owning three great rivers, the Nelson and Mackenzie absolutely, and the St. Lawrence jointly with the United States, although it is practically ours. I do not wish to say anything to make the United States suspicious, but it is patent that we hold the key to the great inland lakes, and we believe that our neighbours will not only help this project forward, but we will assess them on the basis of tonnage so the scheme will pay for itself. As some authorities have said, we could scrap it after a year's operations. But we of course would not do that. We believe that the Americans will pay towards the deepening of this waterway and also contribute
LMr. Baldwin.]
towards its maintenance on a percentage basis. I would not for one moment defend this proposition if I thought it would mean increasing our national debt, but I fully believe that it would be good policy to proceed with this undertaking which would be to the great advantage of the country and without being a great burden on our shoulders. Think of the cheapening of food brought down from the West for the benefit of the East;, and think of the corresponding benefit to the West from Nova Scotia coal being carried direct to the head of the Lakes.
Then this development should be undertaken as an indirect benefit, a stimulus to immigration, and we should see to it that in all contracts Canadian labour and Canadian material are used; and I know that we have factories that can make everything requisite for hydro power development.
Then we need cheap labour. When we go down to the vicinity of New York city and see the hundreds of millions of dollars invested in the development of elevated, surface and subway lines of railway we can only regret that we also have not a similar development. We know that all that was done with cheap labour. At the present time hydro development costs about three to ffour dollars where before the war it only cost one dollar. The last word in hydro-electric power to-day depends on cheap labour. But let this international arrangement be made so that the immense power to be derived from the St. Lawrence river can be developed proportionately for the United States and for Canada, for nothing -will give a greater stimulus to our trade, and nothing will enthuse Canadians more than to see oceangoing boats steaming straight through to the head of the Lakes.
I believe the hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) mentioned the Georgian Bay water system. I must be an optimist, for I believe in that too. But let me assure hon. members that in developing the St. Lawrence route we shall supplement the Georgian Bay project and bring its accomplishment closer. The St. Lawrence route is a necessity for ocean-going boats, while the Georgian Bay route is only suitable for small craft. Therefore, there need be no friction between these two routes, and I am just as much in favour of the Georgian Bay route when the time for it comes, as I am of this route.
A great deal has been said in this House about the high cost of transportation.

We know that it is very high and is adding to the cost of lving. Now, this hydro development will have a tendency to increase our domestic trade for we will not have to go to Pennsylvania for coal when our railways are electrified, and we know that no other country in the world is so well endowed by nature in this respect as is Canada. It makes my heart throb to think of the great potential wealth of this vast country of ours, and I am highly pleased to think that this project is working into shape which will result in the greatest possible expansion from the centre to the circumference of this great country.
I am also in favour of the Hudson Bay route. There is nothing local about me!
We have always said that we are proud of the West, and the building of this canal will help to still further develop the West. We have the finest waterways of any country in the world, and their development must result in making this great country of ours still greater and more prosperous.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Living on the chain of Great Lakes, I naturally take a very keen interest in this question, although, as a Canadian, I should be equally as interested were I not living there. There is one thing that always appeals to me in reference to this project, especially when I hear hon. members asking, as I believe I heard the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) ask a little while ago: Could it be carried out as a commercial proposition? To my mind the answer to that question is to be found in the very strong opposition to this scheme from certain parts of the United States.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will my hon. friend allow me to interrupt him? I did not say that I questioned whether the scheme could be carried out as a commercial proposition. I said that the International Commission would no doubt report on whether it was a commercial proposition or not.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's pqrdon and withdraw my remark, but I understood him the other way. There can be no question that this scheme must be a commercial proposition, because the best minds in this country and in the United States have been brought to bear on the subject, and there would not be such strenuous opposition to it from certain interests in the United States if they did not regard it as a commercial proposition. Providence has placed this great waterway at our disposal, and it is our duty to develop it
as far as we can. It is true that the cost would be great-some estimate it at $100,000,000, others at as high as $300,000,000. I do not say that at the moment Canada is in a position to embark upon an expenditure so great, but I do say that as the result of any expenditure on this account there would be direct returns to the people. To my mind, many expenditures we are making to-day might be cut off and the amounts thus saved applied to a development project of this kind. There is no question of the fact that it would bring about a reduction of freight rates and result in a very great development of electrical energy-and more electrical energy must be developed in this country in order to increase development in the way of manufacturing, the production of fuel, and so on. If these results can be accomplished by the deepening of this water system, the people of Canada will be fairly repaid for any expenditure they make on that account.
A further result from the carrying out of this project would be the development of the ports of Montreal and Quebec-and the development of these ports would result in benefit to the whole country. It has been proved on numerous occasions that small vessels which have crossed the ocean can go up to the head of the Lakes, and it obviously follows that with the deepening of our waterways and the enlargement of our canal system, larger vessels can do the same; bulk will not have to be broken so often, freight rates will go down, and a general benefit will result to the people. This is a question, therefore, that this House and successive Houses must take into their most serious consideration, with a view to seeing whether or not a way can be found to carry out this project. If a committee of this House is not appointed to take evidence, or even to review the evidence already taken by the International Joint Commission, the report of that body may be given little attention, the matter may be shelved and nothing done for some considerable time. This is a live question in many respects; as to the details I do not wish to detain the House now, but it is a question which deeply and vitally affects the interests of the whole people. I therefore have very much pleasure in supporting the motion of my hon. friend from Port Arthur.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I am sorry that I have not heard all that has been said during the course of this debate, but I do not think there

should be any lack of unanimity among hon. members with regard to the resolution before the House. A matter of most vital importance in this country is the development of our national resources in such a way that Canada will receive the greatest possible benefit from them. The water-Powers of Canada are unquestionably among the greatest natural resources which the country possesses. They have this enormous advantage over other natural resources: so long as the earth lasts, water will last and water-powers wili exist. It is therefore extremely important, and in the public interest, not only that they should be developed but also that they should be nationally owned and controlled and that the public should get the direct benefit of these vast resources.
It is absolutely necessary for Canada to take such action as will help to get her out of her present state of debt, particularly that vast load of debt which the war has put upon her. The St. Lawrence route is the greatest national resource that Canada has. It has an enormous advantage over every other public work that this country has heretofore undertaken. The development of that route, the making of a depth of thirty feet over the sills in the canals, so that ships drawing thirty feet of water may go up and down the St. Lawrence, will bring about the production of such an amount of electrical energy that the people of Canada will receive by way of rental an amount sufficient to pay the interest on the vast cost of this development. It does not seem, therefore, necessary to argue that as soon as possible a report should be obtained with regard to the matter and data put before Parliament so that intelligent action can be taken. I understand that an international commission has been dealing with the matter, and I assume that at any early day we shall have engineering and other statements which will enable us to form an intelligent idea of what can be done and what the cost will be. There is no doubt that the work would have to be undertaken internationally, because at least thirty-five states of the United States have so far placed themselves on record as being in favour of the project. The State of New York has uniformly opposed the project, but so far as Canada is concerned, the only opposition to it that I have heard has come from the city of Montreal. Well,
I do not think that opposition is serious, because, when all is said and done, the great city of Montreal will undoubtedly benefit as much as the rest of Canada by
[Mr. Bristol.J
this project. The only question in the minds of shipping people is whether this project should be carried out, or whether what is known as the Georgian Bay Canal route would be the better. Now, I have [DOT] heard rmjn who were the best people, so far as I could find, to express an opinion in the matter, say that it would take so long for ships to cover the long canal distance involved in the Georgian Bay route, the rate of speed being necessarily slow, that the thing would be impracticable from a shipping point of view, and that the St. Lawrence route is the natural and the best route for the shipping interests of this country. We can get the coal resources of Cape Breton up to the head of the Lakes only if we carry out this great project of canalizing the St. Lawrence; and what it would mean to the people of Canada to buy practically all their coal in their own country is something which no one can readily compute. But I venture to say that one of the most important things to the people of Eastern Canada is the obtaining of their own coal in Canada from Canadian coal mines. The completion of the project which we have been discussing to-day would put us in such a position that; at least so far as Eastern Canada is concerned, we should not have to depend upon the United States for our chief supply of coal. Moreover, the ships that bring the coal up from the Nova Scotia districts could take grain down there, and that grain could be shipped from Nova Scotia to the Old Country during the winter months.
The importance of this project is so great, in my opinion, that we should give it immediate consideration in the general interests of Canada. It would lead to the cheapening of freight rates from the great West; it would produce from four to five million horse-power right in the centre of Canada, where labour is easily obtained and transportation easily available for the manufactured goods which would be turned out in large quantities as the result of the utilization of these vast water-powers. It would enable us also, as I have said, to get supplies of coal from Nova Scotia to the head of the Lakes; to send our grain down to the eastern ports, and, generally speaking, tc promote the development of our great natural resources.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the addresses that have been delivered with regard to

the resolution now before the House, and I have come to the conclusion that this is another proposal under which the people of Canada are going to be asked to expend an enormous sum of money in' order to develop transportation on our inland waters. I would respectfully ask the House, before reaching a decision on the subject, to consider this question: We have already expended over $400,000,000 on deepening, buoying and lighting our rivers, building- canals, dredging, deepening and lighting our harbours, for the purpose of cheapening the rates on the freight carried on those waters. What has been the result? Simply this, that the more money we spend, the higher go the rates. The rates have been doubled, trebled and quadrupled, and this Parliament has no control. The time has come when we must take a decided stand on this question, and I for one would oppose the expenditure of any large sum of money on this proposition until Parliament has absolute control over the rates that are to be charged on our inland and coastal waters. It is very nice for these gentlemen to get up one after another and say: "Oh well, we will go on and spend this enormous sum of money, three or four hundred million dollars, in carrying out this proposition, and we will give you cheaper rates." That has always been the cry-that was the cry that helped to build the canals. It is the same old cry that men are making who are coming and asking this Government to deepen, buoy and light harbours, deepen rivers and build canals. It is the same old story. We are going on spending tens of millions of dollars in building the Welland canal. What control have we over the freight rates? Absolutely none. Yet, vte meet here session after session, and when a measure is brought in asking the Government to have control over these rates, we sit here and ignore that measure. I hope, before this session is closed, we shall have control at least over the rates on freight - transported on our inland waters. Until such time comes, I question whether it would be wise for us to appoint another committee and go on and see how much we can spend on such a proposition as this. I am in hearty sympathy with any means of developing transportation on our great inland waterways, but I am also in this position that I for one will at least demand that we have control over those waters and over the rates, tolls, and
charges that are made by the vesselmen who operate on those waters.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, it is not my indention to detain the attention of the House at any great length, but I think it is my duty to express my views on the resolution moved by my hon. friend from Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer). I am certainly in favour of all that can be done towards the development of the country, but my opinion is that the motion which is now before the House has no other object than that of preventing the Georgian Bay canal from being built, and this, from my point of view, would be much more in the interests of the country, than would be my hon. friend's proposal. I listened the other day to the remarks made in the House, and from these I infer that if this resolution were adopted, the United States would benefit by the Canadian money which we would spend. I must, say that I am surprised at the new position taken by my hon. friends on the Government side of the House, they who, in 1911, were against any trade with the Americans and who now wish to let the latter take advantage of a Canadian undertaking. I think it would be more reasonable, Mr. Speaker, to make only such expenditure as would be fully helpful to Canada, and I have always understood that the Georgian Bay canal would be built eritirely and exclusively for Canada's benefit. I am astonished at such readiness to spend the large amount which would be required if a committee were appointed to report on the deepening of the St. Lawrence river, when we already have the reports made on the Georgian Bay canal, by most competent engineers, amongst whom, Mr. Sanford Evans; these reports have never been submitted to the House for consideration.
On behalf of my constituents who are interested in the building of the canal, I certainly will object to the hon. member's motion, as also to all the outlay which it would entail. I therefore request that the House adopt the necessary measures, so that the Georgian Bay canal may be built as soon as possible; this undertaking is of special interest to Canada and it would contribute largely to the development of the country.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a project
which is not only of national interest, but of international interest, and when a question of developing the great natural resources of Canada arises, every Canadian

is apt immediately to favour any such development on any occasion, at any time and for whatever purpose it may be intended. During the last twenty-five years many projects have been put forward in Canada; projects which to-day are calling for the serious attention of our people, projects that have not always received, perhaps, the attention they deserve; projects which have been neglected in their development and which have placed Canada to-day in a position which calls for the thoughtful attention of every business man and every tiller of the soil. For the first time in my Parliamentary life, I am not able to agree with my esteemed friend, the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie), who views this project with great equanimity, and who speaks of the great prospects for the development of trade between Nova Scotia and the other Maritime Provinces and the western provinces.
This project, as I have said, is not only national, but international,-and this is the serious point of the question which must cause every Canadian to halt in his decision in order to see what may be the effect upon the nation at large, and not merely a portion of the country which may be more directly affected by the construction of any proposed public work. This project will be for the great benefit of Canada or it will be to the great detriment of Canada. And with our great expanse of country stretching for thousands of miles from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and when we know that our great desire is to make Canada a nation, with every portion of the country as one in its aspirations, the East for the West and the West for the East, I consider that, instead of entering upon such a project as lightly, as I am afraid some of our Canadians are entering upon it, we should pause for a moment and consider its effect, national as well as commercial, facilities which will keep the West and the East together first of all, in order to keep Canada within the Empire, a nation worthy of the name.
It is this commercial dismemberment that attracts my attention today. I was not in the House when my hon. friend from Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) presented his resolution, but I have read his speech in Hansard and I know that he presented his case in the best possible colours and in the best language that could be used. I have also read the remarks of my hon. friend from Regina

(Mr. Cowan), who hopes that by this new route the products of the West will be carried to the ports of the East. Those ports were placed there by the hand of Providence, not especially for the development of the Maritime provinces, but for the benefit of the western .provinces-ports which will be able to take care of all possible development in the West for centuries to come, and will help to build up a united Canada in every possible direction.
This waterway project is an international one, and we know we are in a false position at the present time on account of our traffic going to the United States instead of over Canadian railways. Had the proper attention been given to that great project initiated not so many years ago by the veteran leader of Canada for fifteen years, had the Transcontinental between Winnipeg and Quebec and St. John and Halifax been looked after as it should have been, Canada would not be confronted today with the problem of high freight rates, This problem of freight rates is on our hands because that great project has been neglected by the Government, and it was the only project that could unite Canada East and Canada West by transportation facilities. The products of the Prairie Provinces at the present time are taken to the city of Winnipeg, and then go to a foreign country through United States channels. Our national railways have immense deficits to-day, and next year we will have a deficit of $100,000,000. As a Canadian I believe that the people of this country will appreciate the necessities of the moment, but I do not think they will endorse this project of opening new channels of transportation and further neglecting the one that, if properly handled, would have made Canada a better nation than it is to-day. I sympathize with the Minister of Railways in having to present to Parliament the deficit existing on the National roads to-day, but I say that if the Government that took office in 1911 had been inspired with goodwill towards the Transcontinental and given its attention to the development of the road from Winnipeg to the Maritime provinces, we would not be confronted with the situation that exists to-day. At this time we should consider the best way out of our present difficulties rather than the project my hon. friend from Port Arthur and Kenora proposes, which, however much it might benefit Canada, would be of greater advantage still to the United States. It could not be otherwise, in view of the means the Ameri-

can nation possesses compared with ours. All the traffic of the American West and the Canadian West would go through American channels, just the same as it has done in the past. I do not think my hon. friend the Minister of Railways will contradict me when I say that the deficits on our national railways to-day are due to the fact that we do not use them. I think everybody in the House will agree that we have commanded only forty per cent of the export trade of the West, while the other sixty per cent has gone through United States channels. What we should have done to stop the deficits was, not so much to increase the rates as to get business for the roads instead of allowing that business to go to the United States. Had we commanded ninety-five or one hundred per cent of the traffic from the West in the last five or six years, we would have scarcely any deficits at all on our railways to-day. The problem that should engage our attention to-day is how to secure for our National railways the traffic that originates in Canada, and every possible step should be taken by the Department of Railways and Canals, by the Government, and by this Parliament, to see that every bushel of grain from Winnipeg should be directed along the Transcontinental to Quebec and the harbours of the Maritime provinces. This would mean a saving of from ten to fifteen cents a bushel to the producers of the prairie provinces. That route saves 214 miles of transportation between Winnipeg and Quebec, and equally to St. John and Halifax. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) is very much concerned over the amount of coal he has to use over the road, especially during the winter season. I would tell him that with proper usage of the Transcontinental, he could save ten to fifteen per cent of his coal on the journey from Winnipeg to Quebec. The road was especially built for heavy loads and long hauls, except the last few miles, which this Government degraded with the object, no doubt, of saying that the road was not up to standard. I think every sensible man is convinced that the road as a whole cannot be surpassed, and it is the only link we have to bring the products of the west to the east, and to( transport to the west the products of the east and those that come from across the sea. Nature is there, and the road is there. No one will deny that if you can save a haul of 215 miles on a certain road, it must be cheaper than a longer route. It is simply a matter of judgment, but it
calls for the attention of every one in authority, and for patriotic effort on the part of the Government and Parliament. I think that before going further into transportation problems it would be well for us to undertake, the proper equipment of our railways, so that we might make the fullest use of them, for they are in need of amelioration. The Transcontinental from Winnipeg to Quebec-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: I think the hon. member is quite justified in saying that no expenditure should be incurred for waterway transportation until our railroads are more fully utilized. Up to that point I did not feel it my duty to interrupt the hon. member, but I must point out that he cannot, on this motion, discuss in detail the administration of the railways of Canada.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
No one, Mr. Speaker, is more anxious to obey your rulings than the member for Gloucester. But there is such a close connection between the project under consideration and the question of railways that it is rather difficult for a member who feels strongly that something should be done to improve railway transportation in Canada, not to transgress the ruling you have just made. However, I shall attempt to bring by remarks to a close as speedily as possible.
Let me say that the Georgian Bay canal enlists my sympathy to a greater extent than the deepening of the Lakes, because it is a purely Canadian route. Now, I hope that my hon. and genial friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) will consider this subject in all its bearings and urge upon the House nothing that will not be in the best interests of the whole country. I should not like to see this country embark on any scheme that might not be commercially wise, nor commendable from the standpoint of patriotism. While I do not say that the proposal before the House is one that does not deserve consideration, I do say that it is one which the people of Canada can well afford to let stand in abeyance until we have placed our railways in a better position and have been able to reduce freight rates through the better operation of the roads. I hope my hon. friend the Minister of Railways is considering the improvement of our railways, and until this is done I do not think other things should be attempted. I cannot support the motion.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I fear I shall be open to the same criticism

which the previous speaker encountered by discussing the railway question when a canal proposition is under consideration. But that hon. gentleman (Mr. Turgeon) has brought before the House an important fact, namely, that we have an immense expenditure in this country in connection with our railways and that we are now seeking to improve our railway system by consolidations. While I have a good deal of sympathy with the idea of improving our transportation by waterway, by better canalization of the lakes and rivers, I say that the urgent need in this country to-day in regard to transportation is the immediate consolidation of the railways, to the end that freight rates may be reduced, as proposed by the hon. member who has just spoken. I hope that before this debate is over, indeed within the next two or three weeks, we shall have an announcement from the Government that they do intend, almost immediately, to consolidate our railway systems and so bring the relief to transportation which is loudly called for at the present time by farmers of the West and by residents of all portions of Canada.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: What does consolidation mean?

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: It means what it ought to mean,-great economy, great efficiency, and other desirable things of that kind, not to mention lower freight rates.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Consolidation of what roads?

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: The roads we have taken over but which we have not yet consolidated.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: I think the House will immediately realize that the speaker was more or less justified in ruling that the administration of our railways should not be widely discussed upon this resolution. I must ask the hon. member to confine his remarks as far as possible to the question of waterways development.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: I agree with you, Mr. Speaker, but my hon. friend opposite tried to lead me aside.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
He tried to make me wander from the subject. I take it that the subject before the House is this, that we are trying to improve our waterway transportation, and it is a very expensive proposition. The canalization involved, harbour improvements, the building of ships

of one kind and another, must appeal to hon. gentlemen as matters that would entail considerable expenditures. And in these times, when the country has such an enormous debt and has so many obligations to meet, if we cannot at present improve our transportation by way of this expensive proposition we can at least do something to reduce transportation charges by the improvement of our railway service, an improvement that is due and ought to be carried out almost immediately. The criticism in the country to-day is that we are under enormous expenses in connection with our railways, and that we have great deficits; and, therefore, if we cannot just for the moment go into the expensive proposition of deeper channels, new canals, improved harbours, and so forth, the Government and this parliament ought to do something immediately in the direction of reducing freight charges in Canada by the amalgamation and the co-ordination of the railroads which we now have, for their diversified administration as well as the duplications that exist represent a great waste of money. I might say on behalf of the people of Ontario that we have every sympathy with the proposal to deepen waterways and also the proposal to increase power development, which would come from the deepening of our rivers and canals. I agree with what has been said to-day as to the enormous electrical energy that could be developed in connection with these deeper waterways, and while it would not mean an entire settlement of the proposition, the Government could take up any day the first great development, namely, that between Montreal and the lower end of Lake Ontario, and in that way we should have a great source of power and be able to bring sea-going vessels into Lake Ontario. Now, if this scheme is a good one, and if you can bring ships right up Lake Ontario, you have proved the whole case. But if that preliminary part of the scheme fails, there is no need to go on. The thing that should be undertaken now, and perhaps we can do it by reason of the great demand for electrical energy, is, by co-operation on the part of the Government with the United States, to carry out an improvement at the lower end of the St. Lawrence and thus allow steamships to get to Lake Ontario. If that proved successful we should be justified in going further. These are questions connected with transportation that notwithstanding our great commitments,

must be dealt with. They ought to be dealt with now, and now to my mind is the time to press for some kind of co-operation between the Government of the United States and the Government of Canada in the direction of deeping our waterways system.

speakeroldname: Mr. SAMUEL WILLIAM JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) :
maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I think the discussion during the past day or two on the resolution introduced by my hon. friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) indicates as clearly as could possibly be indicated that a general election is impending. Within the last thirty or thirty-five years, which is as far as I can remember, when we have had discussion on the Georgian Bay canal in the House and in the newspapers of the government of the day, that was invariably followed by a general election. Engineers were located in different parts of the country, mostly in doubtful constituencies, with mysterious looking tripods and other instruments for the purpose of influencing the electorate. To use a rather slang expression the government used to "get away with it." But to-day it seems to me that that old trick is played out. My hon. friend from Port Arthur coming from a region which perhaps is a little more backward than the constituencies farther east from which some of us come, probably thinks that the people of that district can be induced to vote for the Government on representations such as those made by the member supporting the Government. Otherwise I cannot see why such a resolution as this should be introduced at this juncture following the bringing down of the Estimates which indicate that we have to provide for expenditures of something in the region of $600,000,000. That was more than twice what the national debt of Canada was seven or eight years ago. To-day we have to provide for $609,000,000, notwithstanding that my hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) told us blandly that before the war $100,000,000 or $160,000,000 meant a great deal. Now, said he, we have got accustomed to spending such vast sums it does not mean as much as it did at that time. Well, that is a curious kind of reasoning. Before we spent that two billions of dollars we had it, and we could have spent it very much better than we can now because we have not got it. But notwithstanding that these two gentlemen from the Twin cities-who think in pairs and hunt in pairs-for reasons best known to themselves are advocating the expenditure
of enormous sums of money in the face of the crushing debt the interest upon which' we have to meet. Physicians tell us, Mr. Speaker, that the first symptoms of paresis, a form of insanity well known, is the hallucination of the patient that he is possessed of illimitable sums of money, he proceeds to squander it in a reckless way and in due course he is examined mentally and is sent to an asylum. Now if the Government does not take care some person will have to examine them mentally and see that they are put in a place where they cannot lavishly spend the money of the people of this country. The scheme, so far as I can see, is one of the wildest that has been brought before the House-having regard to all the circumstances-since I have had the honour of being a member of it. In face of the fact that we are overbuilt in the matter of railways and will not be able to catch up for the next twenty-five or thirty years, in the face of the fact that the Estimates already brought down contain a vote of $140,000,000 to provide for these
5 p.m. railways-and I understand that during the recess an Order in Council for an expenditure of something like $77,000,000 was obtained by the Government for the purpose of keeping these railways running-I say in the face of that, it is a foolhardy thing on the part of any member to get up and advocate a matter of this kind even in an academic way. We ought to be brought to our senses in the matter of expenditure of money; and representing as I do the city of Montreal, which contains within its borders something like ten per cent of the entire population of Canada, I cannot allow this resolution to be placed before the House without getting up and most strenuously objecting to it.
Mr. JOHN A. MAHARG (Maple Creek) : I do not want to be considered as knocking this scheme at all. In my opinion there is considerable merit in the project that is outlined in the resolution but, I think, there are other conditions t'hat we must first take into consideration. In my opinion the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) hit the nail squarely on the head in the few remarks that he made which had reference to the control of the shipping on our Great Lakes. I do not know whether the conditions that exist at the present time in that regard are generally known or not. It is very well known to the grain trade however; and I do not think we are confronted with a bigger combine anywhere on the North American con-

tinent than the one we have to deal with in the shipment of our grain across the Great Lakes. The difficulty is not merely in connection with the freight charges; but a combination exists in connection with insurance and boat space that you cannot possibly get away from. You have got to secure your insurance in connection with your boat space or you do not get your boat space at all; and the rates that you are paying run from twenty-five to thirty per cent more than an individual could get insurance for providing he could secure boat space. Now, that is a condition that should not exist. If the Government are aware of that, I think they are somewhat dilatory in the performance of their duty in not at least attempting to remedy such a situation. Surely we should not be compelled to pay that excessive insurance we are compelled to pay by having to take insurance in conjunction with the boat space. That the two requirements should go together is bad enough; but when it becomes a case of paying twenty-five or thirty-five per cent more than you could obtain your insurance for otherwise if you could secure your boat space, then I think it is time for drastic, and very drastic action to be taken. We quite realize that the question of transportation, in so far as the West is concerned, is a very important one, very important; and water transportation should be of the utmost importance providing that we have control. But, as the member for East Lambton said, why should we continue expending millions and millions of dollars every year, as we are now doing and get absolutely no benefit from it. Rates are going up, and up, and up, and to-day they are about three times what they were a few years ago. A year ago they were about four times what they formerly were. Now, Sir, this combine not only goes to the extent of compelling you to take insurance but they absolutely refuse to move. Why, I have it on good authority that the combine in question even held up the Canada Wheat Board for days and days before they would accept shipment because they could not get the conditions that they asked for. When a combine will hold up a Board that has the Government behind it, what treatment is an individual likely to receive from an organization of that nature. In so far as the West is concerned it is not to-day a matter of water transportation. As regards getting our grain out the facilities are there. They take the grain and take [DOT] 
it much faster than the railroads can get it to the lakes. There has never been a time that I know of that the terminal elevators have ever been full during navigation, or anywhere near full. It has generally been the case that only a very small percentage of the space at the head of the lakes has been occupied by grain when navigation closed. We lost in the West this year through lack of railway transportation far more than we could hope to gain even if we had this increased service and control over the rates. It was quite a common instance for seven, eight, ten and twelve cents, and in fact up as high as fifteen cents a bushel, more to be paid for grain where you had assurance that you could get it forwarded to the head of the Lakes at once as against taking a chance of having it forwarded one, two, three or even four months later.
The House may not be aware of all the features of the grain grade. It is not the price paid for grain, that is, cash grain in store or on track, that governs the price paid to the individual delivering on the railroad. The price he is paid for his grain is the price at which some one will purchase from you for future delivery. That delivery may be one, two, or three months hence. It is not contingent on the cash price at all, and if you were delivering grain to an elevator on a line railway where the buyer knows he is not going to gel it out for, say, three months, then he has tc pay the price that some one will pay him for that grain for delivery three months hence. That accounts for the discrepency. It is not the fault of the grain man at all. He is the victim of circumstances and can only pay the price that he can sell that grain for at the time he can make delivery of it. The contention has been made that the sooner the grain is got out of the country the better. That applies particularly to the interior. Get your grain out from the interior if you can, but immediately you get it to the head of the Lakes you have the Government guarantee of its quality and you have no difficulty in financing. But to my mind it is questionable whether it is advisable to throw all your grain on the European markets in one or two months, as the advocates of this scheme recommend. We have not had any trouble in getting our grain from the head of the Lakes; our trouble has been to get it to the head of the Lakes. Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I think it will be wise to withhold further action on this project for some little time. If there is any money to spend, so far as the West

is concerned, I think railway improvements would be of much more value to us at the present time than increased water transportation.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to ask a question of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Keefer) who, I presume, will close the debate, rather than to offer any argument. I notice that his resolution calls for the appointment of a committee to make an investigation as to the benefits to be derived from such a scheme.
I think we all know pretty well what the benefits will be, we know they will be great, but what we are more interested in just now is the cost, and it seems to me that if my hon. friend would add that to the scope of the investigation he would be enormously increasing the benefit to be derived from it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
I would direct the
attention of the House to the circumstance that the mover will close the debate, and therefore, if any other hon. members desire to speak they should do so now.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take any part in this debate, hut in view of the way in which work is duplicated by various departments of the Government, and of the bad example set in that regard by Parliament itself, I want to say a few words. Let me begin by congratulating the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) for the position he took the other evening in regard to this motion, when he pointed out that not only the work that it is proposed to have done by the terms of this resolution but very much more extensive work is at the present time being done by the International Joint Waterways Commission. For that reason the Minister of Railways and Canals urged upon the hon. gentleman who presented this motion, and supported it in a very interesting speech, the propriety of withdrawing it instead of pressing it forward at the present time. No more timely and wholesome advice than that could possibly be given in view of the financial condition of the country and of the burdens that rest upon it, some of which are outlined in the Estimates that have already been presented to the House. As I said a moment ago, it was not my intention to intervene in this debate, but as the discussion has wandered so far afield and so many opinions, interesting and otherwise, have been vouchsafed regarding transportation generally and the carriage of water-borne goods, I may be permitted, Sir, without infringing any of the rules of the House, to follow for a few minutes the bad example set by some of my colleagues on both sides of the Chamber. For that reason, I desire to allude very briefly to that feature of the dis-cfission which compared the benefits of the extension and deepening of the St. Lawrence channel with that of the Ottawa and its tributaries which were referred to as the Georgian Bay canal project. The Georgian Bay canal project has been very fully gone into by a committee of engineers, appointed with the sanction of Parliament and under the direction of a previous government. Investigation was carried on for some years, and in the end a very comprehensive report was made. That investigation and report cost this country a very large amount of money, and it would be just as unreasonable I submit, at this date, to propose that that work be done over again by another committee as it is to propose that a special committee of this House should be appointed to ascertain certain things which, if they have not already been ascertained, will be ascertained in a very short time by the members of the International Joint Waterways Commission. By reason of the fact that the report made by the Georgian Pay Canal Commission may not be familiar to hon. members who at the present time occupy seats in this House, and in view of certain statements in regard to it that have been made in the course of this debate, I would like, for a few moments to direct the attention of the House to some of the findings of the board of eminent engineers which was appointed to investigate that project. In the first place they reported as a result of their investigation:
That a 22-foot waterway for the largest lake boats (600 ft. X 60 ft. x 20 ft. draft) can be established for one hundred million dollars in ten years, and that the annual maintenance will be approximately $900,000, including the operation of storage reservoirs for the better distribution of the flood waters of the Ottawa river.
Then a further finding was set forth in a subsequent paragraph as follows:
That sufficient water may be stored within its own and adjacent watersheds to Operate a summit level above Lake Nipisslng. That to use the Lake Nipissing level as a summit would increase the cost at least $10,000,000 and introduce 12 additional miles of canal cutting.
A still further finding in the same report was in these words:

That the probable^ time taken by a lake freight boat of 12-mile maximum speed, without delays at locks or in meeting other boats, from French River harbour to Montreal would be 70 hours. That the season of navigation will average 210 days from May to November.
And later on in the report it was stated:
That with a storage system as planned, and the tributary basins thereto required for the navigation project, a reliable water-power supply is secured at various dams amounting to 1,000,000 horse-power, which can be developed for about $50 per horse-power.
And finally, there was the following declaration in that report:
That no international waters are aifected.
That feature, Sir-the one I have last mentioned-was one that commended the report to a great many people in this country, and it was a feature which was alluded to the other evening by my friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), and I think, by my friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) in the course of their admirable addresses on this resolution.
Now, let me point out further, Sir, that a great portion of the water-power which this committee found could be developed, is located within easy transmission distance of the territory that would be served from the St. Lawrence. In the first place we have at the Little Chaudiere and Desch-enes at Ottawa, 45,000 horse-power; at Hawkesbury, 65 miles east of Ottawa, 71,000 horse-power; at Point Fortune, 75 miles east of Ottawa, 148,000 horse-power; at the Chats, 30 miles west of Ottawa, 113,000 horse-power; at the Chenaux, 50 miles west of Ottawa, 68,000 horse-power; at Calumet, 63 miles west of Ottawa; 56,000 horsepower; at Rocher Fendu No. 1 and Rocher Fendu No. 2, 65 miles west of Ottawa, 78,000 horse-power; at Paquette Alumette, 85 miles west of Ottawa, 25,000 horsepower; at Des Joachims, 140 miles west of Ottawa, 60,000 horse-power; at Rocher Capitaine, 160 miles west of Ottawa, 80,000 horse-power; at Deux Rivieres, 170 miles west of Ottawa, 38,000 horse-power-or a total in the group I have just mentioned of 782,000 horse-power. In addition to these there are several smaller groups of water-powers, aggregating, according to reliable engineers, about 1,500,000 horsepower. Now, the point I want to make in connection with this group of powers is this: any one of these can be developed for a comparatively small sum of money and would supply the area to be supplied by the development of power on the St. Lawrence, while, on the other hand, accord-[Mt. Murphy.]
ing to eminent engineers, the work on the St. Lawrence would involve the development of four or five blocks of 1,000,000 horse-power each at an expense that is absolutely staggering. That is apparent from the fact that a complete waterway of 30 feet could not be secured on the St. Lawrence for even one ocean going vessel until four or five such power developments had been made. And even if one such block of horse-power were developed, it would merely serve a territory which could be reached by these smaller powers on the Ottawa river and its tributaries.
In this connection some very interesting evidence was given before the International Joint Commission at one of the sessions held last fall, I think it was, in the city of New York, in pursuance of the instructions contained in the letter from the Government to the chairman of the International Joint Commission which was read in this House the other evening by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid). At that meeting one of the most eminent engineering firms in America stated that the cost of developing the St. Lawrence river at one point alone would be $550,000,000, exclusive of the cost of all the shore works and the damages for flooding. Moreover, according to the Minister of Railways-indeed, I think also according to my friend, the member for Port Arthur, who introduced this resolution-there are four or five other such points om the St. Lawrence where the development would be in quantity such as the one I have mentioned and that would cost approximately $550,000,000 in each case.
So that, Mr. Speaker, having regard to the point first raised in this debate by the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and emphasized by subsequent speakers, it is preposterous at the present tima to talk of any such expenditure as would be involved in a scheme of this kind.
However, it is quite true that the resolution of my hon. friend does not propose that this work be proceeded with; it merely proposes an investigation to see what benefits would be derived if such a development were carried out. But as has been pointed out by previous speakers, the appointment of such a committee, with power to sit during the recess, examine witnesses, travel about from place to place and conduct a general roaming inquiry, would of itself involve the expenditure of a sum of money which this Parliament, if it retains its sober senses, would under no circum-

stances think of authorizing. For that reason, Sir, and without going into the merits of these, rival schemes, but having given the House some statistics for the purposes of comparison, I desire to express my entire concurrence with the suggestion of the hon. Minister of Railways that all good purposes would be served, at the present time in any event, by the withdrawal of this motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. H. KEEFER (Port Arthur and Kenora) :
maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that the object of this motion has been well attained in the full discussion that has taken place thereon. I do not intend to reply to all the different arguments that have been advanced or to refer to all the points that have been raised during the course of the debate; I shall simply touch upon two or three of them. In a general way I might say that with the exception of the remarks of the member for the Cartier division of Montreal (Mr. Jacobs), the whole of the discussion has been favourable to the carrying out of the project, provided certain contingencies were concurrent. The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier, however, labels the project a foolhardy proposition. I am glad to know that he is not backed up by his city in that respect. I had the pleasure of attending the sitting of the International Joint Commission in Montreal, upon which occasion the city of Montreal took a much wider and wiser view of the matter, one based upon the general benefit which would accrue to the country as the result of the carrying out of this project. The remarks of the member for the Cartier division of Montreal were very much like the views expressed in Buffalo and in New York in opposition to the scheme -and I cannot help feeling that there was a certain amount of selfish interest in the opposition that came from those quarters. Be that as it may, the city of Montreal took a broad view at the public hearing held by the Commission, believing that the carrying out of the project would result in benefit to Montreal as well as to Canada generally. Montreal is able to look beyond its mountain to the West and to realize what the general benefit will be to Canada as well as to herself.
