I may add that it was not necessary to call in the doctor to examine any of their heads, because they took a sane view of the matter.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that the city of Montreal said this and said that. Who was "the city of Montreal"?
48	*

maintopic: GREAT LAKES-ST. LAWRENCE DEEP WATERWAY TRANSPORTATION
speechtext:
Different organizations were represented, including the Board of Trade. The hon. member for Bonaven-ture (Mr. Marcil) extended a welcome on behalf of the city itself and made the remarks to which I refer with respect to the attitude of the city of Montreal. The only ones who were opposed to it, so far as I heard, were some shipping interests that did not want to have any shipping go past Montreal. The general trend of opinion in that city, however, was in favour of it.
The objection has been raised that any committee appointed under this resolution, would, in its operations, interfere with the work being carried on in regard to this matter by the International Joint Commission. That never was intended, and I stated so in my opening remarks. The idea in view is that when the Commission make their report, when they submit their findings or recommendations and tender the evidence which they heard, a committee of this House will be available to receive that report and look intc it and see that it is distributed among members of the House instead of being consigned to the waste paper basket, as might otherwise be the case. The remarks of the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) in that respect were quite apropos. It was never intended-although the resolution is so worded, I must confess-that this committee should attempt to hear evidence on the subject while the International Joint Commission were doing the same work.
The other objection I have heard stated is that the carrying out of this project might interfere with our Canadian National railway receipts; that we have a large amount invested in our railways and must do nothing to interfere with their revenues. Well, in a sense that is a good argument, though it is not sound argument if- we are asked to continue to have people pay extravagant freight rates when they could get their goods forwarded for one-tenth of the rail freight cost. But the point I want to make is that those who object to the proposal on this ground have entirely missed the point of the problem -that this is a water proposition, a proposal for the improvement of water routes, and therefore involving a decrease of water rates only and having no affect upon railway receipts. Everybody will admit that at no time when a water route is available will a person ship by rail, because the cost of shipping by rail is many times as much as by water



You can bring wheat down from Port Col-borne by water for 5 cents, whereas, it costs much more by rail. Nobody would think of shipping by rail in the summer time, so that this project does not compete against railway transportation. It does, however, reduce the cost, as has been stated, of water-borne transportation during the summer months by the amount which has been stated and which has not been controverted. I have here letters from presidents of United States railways, stating that the improvement and development of this scheme will increase their receipts. Why? To-day practically everything is being taken down to New York and Boston and shipped out from those ports, and the result is that the cars are tied up. The cry is "No cars." There is a loss on those cars, a loss of earning power. They are held waiting for return cargoes, or they come back empty a long distance to the West. They all pile in at the eastern seaboard at a certain time, at the close of the year; and these gentlemen point out that, if they had several seaports, especially at a shorter distance, to which the railways could haul their cars, as they do to Port Arthur and Fort William in the summer time, they would avoid that unnecessary cost and loss. They point out that by this process you open up 2,000 miles of additional ocean navigation, and you have many additional ports to which the railways can haul freight and quickly return for more. As regards our Canadian railways, the latter advantage is not so applicable; but the point is this: In the summer time you do not see the wheat brought by rail around the north shore of Lake Superior on any of the three transcontinental railways. In the winter time this question cannot affect the railways, because the water route is not open; there is no competition. Whatever the railway is and whatever the receipts are, those receipts during the winter will come in. I cannot, therefore, see the force of the objection that this is in any way going to decrease the receipts of our national railways, but I can see how it is going to increase their receipts. At the present time, many products of the North West would come out if they could profitably rise over the top of the rates, unnecessarily high by water. Lower the rates and those products will come out and be hauled down to the head of the Great Lakes and our railways will then get those additional receipts. Therefore, I say that this work when completed will increase the receipts

of our national transcontinental railways. In the winter time very little wheat is hauled by rail around the shores of Lake Superior. During the war quite a quantity was brought down at a considerable cost, but the experience is that, on account of the locomotives being able to haul only half the number of cars and the additional loss of time, it is not a profitable business to be hauling unnecessarily in the winter time around Lake Superior. If this project is carried out, the receipts of our railways will be increased and the quantity of products coming out from the West will also be increased. You will increase in every respect the volume of the trade of the railways, and that is what is desired. We shall then not have so much the cry: "Where are the cars? Where are the new cars that have been asked for in this House?" They will be out in the West doing their work instead of lying idle at the seaboard. And furthermore, much can be saved in additional rolling stock now required to be produced. It is, therefore, a sound policy for Canada, notwithstanding a large expenditure for railways, as quickly as she can to get this canal built so as to increase the receipts of her railways and save capital expenditures that would otherwise be required.
It has been stated that, with the enormous debt that we have upon our shoulders, this is no time to contemplate making any new expenditures. My friend the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), for whom I have a great respect, jocularly said that this project had been brought forward at a time when there was the prospect of an election. Two years ago Canada sent two Cabinet Ministers to Washington in an endeavour to get this matter referred to the International Waterways Commission. The present Prime Minister and the late Hon. Mr. Sifton, went there along with some officials, but nothing was done. But when the Western States arose in their strength and in their own interest on account of the produce of the farmers being unnecessarily taxed by high freight rates, demanded of Washington, that this matter be referred to the International Waterways Commission, then the matter was so referred. Two years ago a communication came from the United States, when no election was in sight. Canada dealt with that communication and suggested that engineers from both countries be appointed to prepare the proper and necessary questions of reference to the International Joint Commission. Each

country appointed an engineer; those engineers met and framed the questions that were frequently transmitted by the letter read by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid). Orders in Council were then passed authorizing the reference, and in that way the whole matter was, by Canada and by the United States, referred to the International Commission to investigate, and we shall soon have that report. But it is very surprising, listening to some of the remarks made in this House, to realize what an utter lack of information there is upon this important subject, and it was with the sole object of getting this matter from this International Commission by its report to the attention of the members through a committee, that this motion has been made.
Another objection has been made-"Oh there is an alternative route, the Georgian bay." There are two routes to the West, and I am not going to argue particularly in favour of one or the other. As the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) said, as long as we can get transportation through without breaking bulk to the head of the lakes, so that the products will not be charged as high as at present in getting them to the market, we are content; it makes no difference whether it is by the Georgian bay route or by this other route. But I remember the criticism of the hon. member from Marquette (Mr. Crerar), which was to the effect that this project is, perhaps, not advisable. He did not say that it was not; but he went on to say that freight rates depend upon the return cargoes, and you must have the return cargoes. It is for that reason that I was endeavouring to accentuate the point that there were return cargoes, I refered in opening this matter to the boats going in and out of Manchester to take cargoes in and bring cargoes out. In this case, when this canal is opened up, there would be many .cities from which cargoes could be had, such as Buffalo, Cleveland, Detroit and Chicago. The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) said that I said nothing of the Canadian cities. I beg his pardon. I mentioned, "and the Ontario ports". We shall have all those places on the American side and on the Canadian side. Ontario is surrounded on the south by water; it is her boundary all the way until you get practically to Manitoba, and all the busy cities and towns of Ontario will have freight to send out and be able to receive freight from overseas. There is your return cargo to and from Canada; but the point is this,
48i
in answer to the hon. member for Marquette -he will also have his return cargo which is to-day going to and being received by the seaports of New York and Boston. WThy? Where do these goods go to? To New York? No, they go to Chicago, Indianapolis, St. Paul, Minneapolis, Milwaukee, Detroit, Wisconsin, Indiana. Now we will have ocean tramp steamers coming into those upper lakes on account of that class of business and there will be no difficulty at all, after having brought their cargo in and discharging, in their making the short journey either to Chicago, Duluth, Port Arthur, or Fort William, and loading up with grain or any other agricultural products. Because of that we will have these return cargoes, and therefore it is that those who have given the matter the most consideration realize that the immediate construction of this waterway would be in the national interests. There is the further fact that we have spent millions on the Welland canal, which will be useless unless it is connected up with the Port of Montreal.
There are other reasons that could be urged by those who have studied the question of the Georgian Bay and the St. Lawrence. The St. Lawrence is primarily a navigation proposition. Secondly, it is a power proposition. The St. Lawrence river is the most remarkable river in the world so far as navigation is concerned. No other river in the world has such a steady constant flow. The St. Lawrence never varies in one year more than 1 [DOT] 2 feet. Nature has built immense reservoirs and dams like our inland lakes, which would have cost an enormous sum for man to build. The waters flowing from the different rivers, the Kaministiqua, the Nipigon, the White river, the Michipicoten, etc., settle down in the lakes to a clear blue water, not carrying any sediment. These settling works have already been constructed. The river never varies in the springtime. Compare that with the Ottawa river. We must stopthat rise and fall of 20 feet every year; then when we have done that, we will be able to say it may become a ship canal; it is a ship canal we are after, not a barge canal. Experience teaches us that ships will take short canals for long water stretches, but that they will not take long canals for the opposite. I cannot understand why hon. members representing the constituencies along the Ottawa river, especially those representing the city of Ottawa, are not in favour of this project. There will only be five locks in the St. Lawrence. Two of these locks must be

built as part of the Georgian Bay or Ottawa river system, to get into the lake St. Louis. Then you would be within six feet of the level of the lake of Two Mountains, which is an enlargement of the Ottawa river, which river here flows into lake St. Louis, which in turn is an enlargement of the St. Lawrence river. Then you could carry on with the Georgian Bay system, from these two locks already then built. I would have thought that any person desiring to see Ottawa become a seaport, to see the Ottawa river developed, to see even the Georgian Bay canal built, would feel that in so doing they were getting two-fifths of the benefit of the St. Lawrence system for their own canal. Those are the facts. I cannot understand any opposition to this project once it is properly understood.
If the International Joint Waterways Commission are dealing only with the St. Lawrence, let this whole question be referred to a committee of the House, and if the other scheme is preferable the House can throw this one out if it sees fit, and take on the other. But let us get the facts, and disseminate them, and then we will know what to do.
As to the question of cost as I said at the outset, we are hard up, we cannot afford to spend money; but if we are spending money at the present time and do not know it we should take that wasteful expenditure by the throat, and that is what we would be doing in this case. I made the assertion in the opening of my remarks, and I still maintain that it is true, that the United States and Canada are losing hundreds of millions of dollars by hot having this canal built. Mr. Julius H. Barnes, formerly president of the United States Grain Corporation, has shown that on the 4,000,000,000 grain^ product of the United States and Canada the producers are losing $200,000,000 annually, and that statement has not been controverted. Add to that the loss on the package freight, and-leaving aside the question of electric power-this project will pay on navigation and navigation alone. If that be so, why should we not pay annually sinking fund, and interest on the capital invested, particularly if it is only one-tenth of the amount that is wasted every year. We would not tolerate that waste if we knew it. Let us get the facts, and I am sure the people of this country will say: Hard-up as we are, we do not want to pay for this waste in freight rates, but would rather pay it straight to

the Federal treasury and have something for it.
With reference to the cost of development of power, the statement made by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) was, I believe, the statement of a New York engineer who was the consulting engineer of the water-power interests. That was the opposition we had in Montreal- the water-power interests. They are not anxious to see the further development of water-powers on the St. Lawrence river, and their policy was to make the cost as great as possible, but let me remind my hon. friend from Russell, who I am sure is aware of it, that the Parliament of Canada heretofore has had a proposition before it from gentlemen of New York State offering to build the canal at that point if they were given the power at the point of which he speaks. They would build the canal locks free of cost to either country if they were handed over the power-this power that we are told now was to cost at this one point, $550,000,000. That proposition nearly got through this House. It got through the New York State legislature. Then application was made to the courts of the United States to quash the whole incorporation of the American Company on the ground that it was ultra viras, that no private company could be given the rights of navigation by the state. This place where $550,000,000 was to be spent for power, we could have had built without it costing Canada anything, if we had seen fit. I do not know just what the $550,000,000 represents, whether it means complete water-power development, machinery and everything else. I dare say it does. I have been told that when you start in and develop water-power, your development cost is, say, $1, for the mere dams and so forth; but for your plant, your houses, your necessary machinery, the living quarters for the men who live there, moving pictures and so on, the cost is $100 to every $1. Probably that $550,000,000 includes all those items.
What I say is that as Canadians we should get to understand this question, just as our cousins to the south now understand it. The only opposition they have over there is the selfish opposition of part of New York State, and of the Buffalo and Erie Canal interests. The people over there now see the benefit of this canal, and let us try to see what benefit there is in it for us also. I have no objection to seeing also what the cost is. Let us

know exactly what it will cost. The hon. member for Quebec said, let us also refer to the committee at the same time the question of getting the grain to Quebec as well as to Montreal all rail. Be it so. He will find that by rail it is ten times the cost it would be by water. Let all these questions be referred to the committee; let us get the facts, and then we can act intelligently. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) was good enough to say that if I withdrew this resolution he would undertake to see that this whole question was referred to one of the standing committees of the House. A committee which I did not know existed at the time I drafted the resolution, namely, the Committee on Forests, Waterways and Water-powers. I should be glad to see the matter go before that committee. There is nothing much that can be done until we have the evidence and the report from the International Joint Commission as a basis to work upon. The report should be presented about the second Tuesday in April next, and under the circumstances I gladly avail myself of the undertaking of the Minister of Railways and withdraw the motion on this understanding.
Motion withdrawn.

speechtext: Resuming the adjourned debate on the proposed resolution of Mr. Smith, that in the opinion of this House it would not be in the interests of Canada should the Government of Great Britain remove the embargo upon cattle going into the United Kingdom, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Pedlow.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock yesterday I moved the adjournment of this debate, and it is rather a coincidence that I should now be tempted again at six o'clock to move its further adjournment. However, I shall not do so, although it is practically time for recess. I shall conclude the remarks which I was addressing to the House yesterday. I was speaking at the time of adjournment on the visit of the Minister of Agriculture of Ontario to Britain in connection with the removal of the embargo, and had expressed the opinion that that visit, instead of assisting in the endeavour to secure its removal, would on the contrary have a prejudicial effect by creating a feeling of resentment on the part of the British people against this country by reason of the interference of a provincial minister in a
matter purely within the decision of the British people. That my opinion is well founded is obvious from the following comment which I shall quote from the London "Morning Post" as reported in the press:
The London Morning Post says: "Mr. Doherty will associate himself with political action here, a proceeding so obviously improper that we can only suppose that the Minister for Ontario has not understood to what he is being committed."
I think we shall all agree that the "Morning Post" has sized up that minister very accurately. Mr. Doherty has said that he is in Great Britain to-day, not as the Minister of Agriculture of Ontario but in his capacity as a private citizen of Canada. He is evidently endeavouring to play the dual role of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde. When he is in Ontario he is the Minister of Agriculture for Ontario, and when he goes to Great Britain on a message relating to agriculture he is a private citizen. I do not think that it will tend to predispose the British people in favour of the removal of this embargo, when a private citizen of Canada goes there to give them counsel gratuitously as to what they ought to do. This has been made a political question. The Labour people have taken it up and are using the removal of the embargo as an argument against the government of Great Britain. What is the reason they give for its removal? Is it because they are anxious to assist the British agriculturists? Not at all. Is it because they want to assist Canadian exporters? By no means. What they want is cheap meat, and it does seem to me that this is not a very strong reason why the Canadian people should desire the removal of the embargo. If the embargo were removed in accordance with the wishes of the Labour people of Britain, it would be removed not only from Canadian cattle but from cattle coming from Argentine and Australia, and it would be hopeless for the Canadian people to think of competing in the British market with the cattle from those countries. The Canadian farmer is in a much better position to-day than he would be in with the removal of the embargo from the cattle of all countries, because, being nearer Great Britain than any of those cattle-producing countries, he can ship his cattle there alive much more freely and expeditiously and to better advantage than the farmers of Australia or the Argentine. We therefore have a sort of preference in the British market in that respect. I

am afraid that the only reputation which the Minister of Agriculture of Ontario will gain in the Old Country will be one that will not he very favourable. He will go down in British history, I fear, by the appellation of "Meddlesome Manning," meddling with things with which he has no business and no concern, and ignoring the proper channel through which this *question should be taken up, namely, the Federal Government. I was struck with the statement yesterday of the Minister *of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) to the effect that of a million cattle annually passing inspection at our abattoirs less than ten per cent are fitted for export to the British Islands to compete there with the cattle of - Australia and Argentine. If that is so, then I think it should be a stimulus to the Canadian farmer to improve his cattle still further. It may be difficult for the farmers of the West to do this, but certainly the farmers of Ontario should be urged, and urged very strongly, to finish their cattle properly so that they can send them in a condition that will secure the approval of the British people. What we need in the livestock industry in Ontario is more intense feeding. That seems to be the principle which the British farmer has followed for years, and it is a good one for the Ontario farmer to emulate. Now, Mr. Speaker, I desire to move an amendment to the amendment to the following effect:
That all the words after the word "that" in the original motion, and all the words of the proposed amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:	"This House
approves and supports the policy of the Government and of previous Governments of Canada in protesting against the implication of disease in Canadian cattle by reason of the maintenance of the embargo thereon by the British Government."
This Government has done all that it possibly can to secure the removal of the embargo. It received a promise from the British Minister of Agriculture in 1917 that the embargo would be removed, and if that promise has not been carried out it is not the fault of the Government. Seconded by the hon. member for Duf-ferin (Mr. Best, I beg to move the amendment to the amendment which I have iust read.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

I do not intend to deal at any great length 	I
with this subject at the present time for the reason that I was not quite ready to do so to-night owing to an understanding I had that it should not be discussed until Monday's sitting, which would have given me more leisure to make further investigation into the matter. There is now before the House the resolution of the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Smith), the amendment moved by myself, and the sub-amendment of the member for South Perth (Mr. Steele). During the time that has elapsed, and during the discussion that has ensued, since I placed my amendment before the House, there seems to have arisen in the minds of some hon. gentlemen a misapprehension as to my motives and as to the aims of my amendment. Let me say distinctly at the outset, Sir, and so that there may be no room whatever left for any misunderstanding, that there was no intention on my part to dictate to the Imperial Government as to the course they should pursue in domestic affairs, and I do not think that any person reading my amendment could come to that conclusion. I moved that amendment at almost the conclusion of the debate on the resolution, and it seemed to me that it Would be rather unfortunate, after so much discussion on an important subject of this kind, if the resolution should be withdrawn without apparently accomplishing anything beyond affording hon. members an opportunity to express their opinions. I therefore briefly outlined my reasons for taking the course I did, and moved my amendment, which reads as follows :
. That all the words after the word "House" m the resolution be struck out and the following inserted in lieu thereof: "The Government of Canada should make a strong protest against the reasons assigned by the British Government that Canadian cattle are diseased as an excuse for placing an embargo on Canadian live cattle going into the United Kingdom".
I do not think that amendment warrants the conclusion that some hon. gentlemen seem to have reached. It certainly was not my intention either to interfere in the pending elections in the Old Country, or to attempt to dictate to the Imperial Government as to what course they should pursue in domestic affairs. But, Sir, we have a grievance that we should voice; and the fact that we have no right to interefere in Imperial affairs does not debar us from protesting to the Imperial Government, if we have a grievance, just as we would protest to the authorities of any other country, had we cause to do so. I do not think that we in Canada should hesitate


in fact I do not think the Imperial Government expects us to do so-to express our disapproval of Imperial action on this question. As a matter of fact, during the whole period covering the years that have passed from 1892 down to the present time, successive Canadian Governments have protested against the unfairness of this embargo on our cattle. In the brief interval since yesterday I have hurriedly read the records and find that government after government have protested against, not the embargo only but the unfairness of the reasons assigned or implied for its imposition. As a matter of fact, there is no room for concluding that, in the early stages at least, the reasons for the embargo were merely implied; they wer specifically stated. I read that many efforts were made during all these years. And what has been accomplished, Mr. ' Speaker? As far as I can learn, practically nothing. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister says that a promise was at last extracted from the British Government. But for what purpose? Simply that this embargo would be removed after the war.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister if in his judgment we are still at war? I know that the great country to the south of us claim that they are still at war with Germany ; and certainly their refusal to repeal certain war-time provisions against the enemy would lead to that conclusion. But so far as Canada is concerned the war ceased on July 9, 1919, and since then the Imperial authorities, one would think, have had ample time to implement their promise.
Now, Sir, I have been challenged by some hon. members, among them my hon. friend for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), to adduce facts in support of my resolution, and that hon. gentleman has stated that if I can produce the data on which I base the conclusions arrived at in my amendment to the resolution he will support me. Therefore I should like to call the attention of the House to some extracts from Sessional Papers, Vol. XXVI, published in 1893. I find away back in that year two unfortunate cows were the beginning of all this trouble, and that from that date down to the present time various governments, both Conservative and Liberal-and I suppose Unionist, too, when it had time to spare for work of that kind-have been dealing with the subject, but without much result. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) informed us the other day that even as late
as a year ago an attempt had been made by the Government to have this embargo removed, but practically nothing was accomplished. I find in a Sessional Paper, dated London, October 24, 1892, the following cablegram:
Two animals, one a cow, ex steamer "Monk-seaton" or "Huronia" at Dundee and Fifeshire slaughtered suspicion pleuro-pneumonia. Postmortem indication very similar pleuro but no decision yet arrived at. Have seen authorities and pointed out impossibility disease being pleuro. Make immediate inquiry where all animals came from. Most important to prove no contact with American cattle and no disease in locality stock came from.
(Signed) Tufper.
From that time on a voluminous correspondence ensued, and Sir Charles Tupper refers again to these unfortunate cows. He writes:
I cannot help thinking it a pity, in any circumstances, that the two "old worn-oiit" cows, to which Dr. McEachran refers as having been shipped by the "Huronia", should ever have been allowed to come over, and I am strongly of the opinion that we should follow the practice of the Danes, who rigorously keep back any animal that is likely to cause suspicion, or require to be examined on landing in this country. We cannot be too careful, in view of tlie difficulties, trouble, expense and anxiety which any case like that at present under consideration causes, and I shall be glad if you will give the matter your attention.
I remain, yours faithfully,
Charles Tupper.
Nothing apparently was accomplished, although protests continued to be made by the Dominion Government. In that respect, you will notice, Mr. Speaker, that I was not finding fault with the Government for not attempting to get the embargo removed, but I was rather impatient at their failure to produce something of value as the result of their efforts. The Edinburgh Scotsman of 5th November, 1892, published the following:
The urgent representations of the great bodies of English agriculturalists have prevailed at the board of agriculture, and Canada is to be deprived of the privilege she has up till now enjoyed of free trade with this country in live cattle. Mr. Herbert Gardner has, at any rate, waited to hear both sides before coming to this decision. The Canadian authorities have, I believe, been .most diligent in their efforts to rebut the suspicion cast upon the Dominion cattle.
The week following that an influential deputation waited upon the president of the British Board of Agriculture in London. The Duke of Westminster in introducing the deputation said:
Mr. Gardner would not have been surprised that they had requested to have this interview with him, on account of the very deep and well founded alarm that had been spread all over

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment moved by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) is, as I heard it read, in the terms suggested by myself yesterday to be substituted for that of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow). But I understood my hon. friend to take exception to that as not being his amendment, and consequently the sub-amendment became necessary. Therefore, as I understand the matter now, it is'the sub-amendment that is before the House.
The only word that I rise to add on this occasion is that I do not think this subject should be seized upon to endeavour to create in Canada a feeling against Great Britain. The hon. member for Red Deer

(Mr. Clark) put the whole subject in a very concise and, as I thought, fair and proper way in the speech he made yesterday. His words, associated with those of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) expressed what I think ought to be the attitude of Parliament towards this question at this time. It would be quite wrong for Parliament to affirm that the British Government assign, as a reason for the maintenance of this embargo, disease amongst Canadian cattle. The British Government, when the embargo was put on some thirty years ago, did so, assigning as a reason then, just as quoted by the hon. member for South Renfrew, that there was suspicion of disease in respect of at least one animal-it may be that my hon. friend is correct in describing the case as that of "two unfortunate cows"
.-in a Canadian shipment, which animal, I understand, had actually come from the United States. It is a fact that now they assign, as at least one of the grounds, if not the only one, for the maintenance of the embargo, the fear that, although our herds to-day are free and have, for many years, been free of disease, nevertheless, contagion may come to their stock through Canada from importations from the United States or otherwise, or from disease subsequently recurring within the herds of Canada. They do not at all assert, nor even venture to suspect, that the herds of this country to-day are not wholly free from disease. Consequently, it would be very unfair on the part of this Parliament to pass an amendment embodying an assertion on our part of something that was not strictly a fact.
But inasmuch as the original embargo arose from suspicion of disease, if not disease on the part of an animal that came with a Canadian herd, the continuance of an embargo, arising from that source, we have claimed, constitutes an implication against Canadian stock. I must say that there are many who think-and from this opinion I am not free myself-that the continuation of this policy in Great Britain is really a measure of protection established by the British Government for the benefit of cattle raisers in the old land. It is not the only measure that has protective effect which the British Government now enforces, to which they have had resort in recent years, and it has often occurred to me that the public opinion that they have created there-and possibly it is better described as a public prejudice-against protective duties, is at the
[Mr. Meighen.J
bottom of the disposition on the part of the Government and Parliament there to resort to other means to get the same result. Consequently, we feel that as they are able to get that result by other means, those other means if any, should be adopted, and they should not continue an embargo that arose from a cause that they know has now passed away.
If they feel that, as was expressed by ' the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), they should continue the embargo for the reason that they want to be doubly sure that there will be no recurrence of disease or no admission of diseased cattle to Canada and, consequently, transmission of the contagion to British cattle, then they should take such appropriate action as will remove the original imputation that has all along attended this embargo and place their policy upon another basis. I think I have expressed with some care and, I believe, exactly, the position that governments in Canada have taken for some time, and this finds expression as well in the sub-amendment moved by the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele). It seems to me that the passing of that sub-amendment is consonant with the historic policy of Canada, with the dignity of Canada and also with the continuous practice of this country to respect the rights of the British Parliament within their own domain. Therefore, I hope the House will accept, as it stands, the sub-amendment, and if possible, that there will be no division of opinion [DOT] upon it.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queen's) :
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the sub-amendment is a vote of confidence in the present Government and in preceding Governments for having protested against this embargo. I am not aware that anybody has attacked the attitude of the present Government or of any preceding Government on that point. Therefore, I do not think the present Government or the preceding government, of which I had the honour to be a member, needs any whitewashing of that kind; but I do not think it does any harm and I have no objection to offer to it.
Will this sub-amendment be communicated to the Imperial Government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. I will see that
the resolution as passed by Parliament is duly transmitted to the High Commissioner, as it is through his office that the representations of this country have been made.
"MARCH 10, 192]

I just wish tc say that the reason why I second and shall support the sub-amendment is this: I believe that the present Government and all former governments in the last 20 or 25 years have tried to do all they could to have the cattle embargo removed. The reason I am opposed to the original resolution is that I think we have no right to dictate to the British Government what shall be done in the matter of the embargo; it is their business, not ours. The reason I am opposed to the amendment is because the British Government, as I think every hon. member is aware, are not claiming that there is disease among our cattle at the present time. While the embargo was put on for that reason in the first place, I fully agree with my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) that we have no authority whatever for saying that the British Government claim now that there is disease among our cattle. We cannot go by newspaper reports and by what people say. I believe that the newspapers and the amendment to the resolution are simply doing harm to our cattle, because the amendment practically says that the British Government is keeping the embargo on because there is disease among our cattle. I repeat, we have no right to dictate to the British Government what laws they shall make, and I do not want the British Government or the government of any other country to dictate to us. I certainly shall not vote to dictate to them.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton and Victoria) :
speechtext:
I do not see that very much is to be gained either by the amendment or by the sub-amendment. There is one thing, however, that I wish to say to the Prime Minister, and to my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), and that is, there is no record of the British Government ever having changed the stand they took on the question of pleuro-pneumonia. They gave as a reason for putting on the embargo, that there was disease among our cattle, and that reason is of record. Now if there is a change in their attitude, that also should be a matter of record with some government of this country, and until the Prime Minister or some other member of the Government can show that the British Government have receded from the stand they took some twenty or more years ago, and that that change of attitude is a matter of record in this country, there is no use talking about it any more. To say that
there has been a change of attitude on the part of the British Government without being able to produce any evidence to that effect, is as futile as it would be for me to stand up in court and say: Such and such is the, decision of the courts on the records, but a case has been decided somewhere that has not been reported, and I ask your lordships to follow that unreported case. Of course, their lordships would tell me at once that they could pay no attention to that unreported case, but would have to follow the reports of the law as they found them. I submit to the Government, and particularly to the Minister of Agriculture, that we have no record that the British Government have changed their minds, and until they have reversed what they unjustly said about our stock, we cannot very well say that the matter has been fully cleared up.
I think there is very litle difference, Mr. Speaker, between the amendment and the sub-amendment. I am sorry that even in these little things there must be fault found and that the Government has apparently reached the conclusion that no good thing can come out of Nazareth at all. They would not suggest to my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) that he change a word or two in his amendment, but if there was any credit to be gained from action in this matter, his resolution had to be wiped out entirely and one introduced from the other side.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
quite mistaken. I suggested yesterday, and even sent across the floor, this very amendment, but when it appeared to-day as the amendment of the hon. member for South Renfrew, he repudiated it.

The amendment was not made. My right hon. friend is not fair. What got into the report and into the records was a bungle and a mistake. As I understand it, and as will appear by Hansard to-morrow, the thing was simply written on the back of some paper, and the officer of the House who was taking this thing down just took it as if it was all right. The fact of the matter is simply this. The hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Steele) was afraid that the hon. member for South Renfrew would get some kudos out of this thing, so he had to come forward with an amendment of his own. The idea in both is exactly the same; the difference is only a word or two one way or the other, and if we get any results from our action in this matter, I

say that the hon. member for South Renfrew is entitled to the whole credit.
If you will allow me, Mr. Speaker, I should like to correct a mis-statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would rule that the hon. member has the right to correct a mis-statement if one has been made.

I understood the Prime Minister a few moments ago to make the statement that the amendment apparently to be accepted by the House was sent across the floor of the House yesterday evening. If by that he meant that the amendment was sent to myself, his statement is not correct. The Prime Minister, I am sure, does not wish to be unfair. He may have been under the impression that it was delivered to me, but the first time I saw the amendment in its present form was to-night after the House rose at six o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I might say that I had the privilege of occupying the Chair at the time, and I remember distinctly that the amendment was sent across the floor of the House, but it was only sent as far as the front benches on the Opposition side, and read by some hon. member sitting there. I am quite sure it did not reach the hon. member for South Renfrew.

I merely rise to protest against the statement that has been repeatedly made during this debate that there is an embargo against Canadian cattle entering the ports of Great Britain. The embargo is not against Canadian cattle, but against cattle from all countries. The word "Canada" does not appear in it at all, and I am surprised that hon. gentlemen opposite and some hon. members on this side of the House have discussed the embargo as though it were an enactment of the British Government directed particularly against Canadian cattle. When it was first imposed that was the case. In November, 1902, the British Board of Agriculture had the right to prohibit the importation into Great Britain of cattle from any country providing disease was suspected to exist in the herds of that country. In 1904 the Acts of the British Parliament were consolidated, and what was then known as the Diseases of Animals Act came into effect. In 1896, on the 20th of July, the Act that is at present in force in Great Britain came into operation, and that Act applies to all countries. The excep-

tion that is to-day being taken might well have been justified with regard to British legislation from November, 1902, up to July 20th, 1906, but no exception can be taken to the action of the British Government in passing the Act of 1896 as directed solely against Canadian cattle, and I was 'surprised to find in the press again to-day a'reference by one of the provincial Prime Ministers of this country to the matter. We have now three, if not four, of them on record protesting against the embargo on Canadian cattle which has been imposed by the British Government. In order to clear the minds of some of those who apparently are labouring under a misapprehension, I will read section 26 of the Diseases of Animals Act, 1894. The Board of Agriculture were given certain authority under this Act. Section 26 reads:
In relation to foreign animals other than those the landing whereof is for the time being prohibited by order of the Board of Agriculture-
This is the class we were in at that time. Canadian cattle were prohibited in November, 1902, from entry into the interior and were compelled to be slaughtered at the port of landing.
-and other than those brought from the Channel .Islands or the Isle of Man, if and so long as the Board are satisfied with respect to any country out of the United Kingdom or any specified part of such country that the laws thereof relating to the importation and exportation of animals, and to the prevention of the introduction or spreading of disease, and the general sanitary condition of animals therein, are such as to afford reasonable security against the importation therefrom of diseased animals, the Board, by order, shall allow animals or any specified kind of animals, brought from that country or such part to be landed without being subject to the provisions of the Third Schedule to this Act as to slaughter or quarantine, and may for that purpose alter or add to those provisions as the case may require.
Provided that the admission of such animals sail be subject to such regulations as to the route by which the animals are conveyed to this country, quarantine or otherwise, as the Board of Agriculture may by order direct.
The Board of Agriculture were given a certain latitude to exercise their own judgment in matters of this kind. But as I have already pointed out, on the 20th of July, 1896, the British Government passed an Act, which reads:
An Act to amend the Diseases of Animals Act, 1894 (20th July, 1896). Be it enacted by the Queen's most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords, Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same ; as follows:
1. (1) For section twenty-four of the Diseases of Animals Act, 1894, shall be substituted the following section, namely;

Now, I would ask the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) to pay particular attention to this provision, which covers cattle such as were taken in from Holland for exhibition purposes.
The provisions set forth in part 1 (slaughter at port of landing-) of the Third Schedule to this Act shall apply to all foreign animals other than-
(a)	foreign animals the landing of which is for the time being prohibited by order of the Board of Agriculture ; and
(b)	foreign animals intended for exhibition or other exceptional purposes,-
The very class of cattle alluded to by the hon. member for South Renfrew.
-and the landing of which is allowed for the time being by the Board, subject to the provisions of Part 2 (quarantine) of the Third Schedule to this Act.
(2) Section twenty-six of the Diseases of Animals Act, 1894, is hereby repealed.
Now, this is the law in Great Britain, and the name of Canada is nowhere to be found in it; is not even considered in the matter. The Act is one to protect the herds of Great Britain from the possibility of the introduction of disease, and it has been consistently maintained by the British Government from that day to the present; and the governments of this country, both present and past, have been continually taking this matter up, as they were justified in doing. I have no doubt that they did everything possible to induce the British Government to consider the matter favourably from our standpoint, and in fact I know that such has been the case. In view of this fact, therefore, I think it is very unfair and, indeed, undignified on the part of any individual or Provincial Government of this country to do anything or take any action that would have the effect of embarrassing the Government of Great Britain at the present time. Prom the character of the agitation that is now on foot, and the meetings that are being held, it is obvious what the object is. Do you believe that this agitation to have the embargo removed is due to any consideration for the welfare of this country? Is it due to an honest desire to free our cattle from a supposed stigma? If that were the case I think that different methods would be adopted and the matter would be properly urged upon the British authorities. But we had the spectacle of the Minister of Finance of Ontario addressing a meeting in Western Ontario less than two weeks ago, when he pointed out what was likely to happen, and said that if the embargo were lifted the full credit would go to the Hon. Manning Doherty. The Provincial Minister
of Agriculture. He endeavours to forestall a possible event in the future and to appropriate to a member of the Ontario Government the full credit therefor. I think that the attitude of those hon. gentlemen who are even now anticipating the removal of the embargo and trying to claim in advance full credit for it shows exactly what their whole object is. Now, I do not desire to prolong this discussion. I expressed myself yesterday on the subject, and I rise on this occasion only to remove the impression, if it still remains in the minds of any hon. gentleman, that the British authorities have an embargo on the cattle of this country exclusively on account of disease in our herds. In 1902 an embargo was placed on Canadian cattle because of the belief that there was disease, but since 1896 an embargo has rested on all cattle from foreign countries, and it has been purely a protective policy on the part of the Government of Great Britain, not only to protect the livestock interests of that country but also to safeguard them from the introduction of disease into their herds from other countries.

The hon. member who has taken his seat (Mr. Sutherland) seems to see a difference between the attitude of the British Government before and after 1896. I understand that the British Government at the present time does not say that Canadian cattle are diseased. They say in effect: Your means of quarantine, your quarantine organization at the border, is so far from perfect that a stray sick animal from the United States can get in, and that is the reason this law has to apply to you as well as to other parts of the world. I think it has been shown us in the very excellent speech of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) that our quarantine organization is of the best, when of three million animals slaughtered in the Old Country not one showed the diseases complained of. Now, I should like this matter to be treated not as a party question. The Government is doing right, as other governments have done in the past, in protesting against the implication that our cattle are diseased, and if we can hold up their hands in that regard as the united representatives of a united people, who do not want this slander to be perpetuated on any ground whatsoever, whether against our cattle or against our quarantine organization, then I say that we should make our action as non-partisan

as possible and should speak with a united voice against this wrong. I am not going to speak at any length, but I have the honour to represent in this House one of the most purely agricultural counties in the whole Dominion of Canada-
Oh, oh.
-a county which is renowned for its splendid cattle. There is no better butter made in the world than in the hills of the Eastern Townships.
Hear, hear.

Let me repeat that statement. I am always moderate in all my statements, and this is not by any means extravagant. There is no better butter made than in my county. I shall make no comparisons to hurt any one's feelings and so I leave it at that. I think we should speak in a united manner on this question and support the hands of the Government, who are only following the good precedent established by previous governments in urging that this embargo upon cattle coming from this country, where no disease exists and where the quarantine organization is as good as it is, shall be removed.

(Prescott): My hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) objects to the Minister of Agriculture of Ontario taking part in the protest against the embargo. Well, I think that the Government should invite the various provincial governments to help them in their endeavour to have the embargo removed. Even if the embargo does not rest on Canadian cattle only, but on the cattle of all countries, the fact remains that our cattle are under that disadvantage. It has been said that the embargo is not directed against Canadian cattle in particular but is also enforced against cattle coming from other countries. Nevertheless, we have been asking the British Government for many years to remove it but without success. If we now obtain the cooperation of the various Provincial Governments in Canada we will stand a better chance of succeeding. The other day the Legislature of Quebec passed a resolution in favour of the removal of thfe embargo, and I think the Legislature of Alberta adopted a similar course. The Ontario Government is also taking an active part in the movement to have the embargo removed. The Minister of Agriculture for the Province of Ontario, a very active and very capable man, is at present interesting him-
self to that end. He may perhaps carry the agitation into Great Britain itself, but we know that all these obstacles to trade are only removed after a strong agitation; and I would have no objection to the Minister of Agriculture for Ontario conducting a little agitation along the desired lines if it is felt to be necessary. If the embargo is removed I have not the least objection to giving some of the credit to the Minister of Agriculture for Ontario, as well as to the Ministers of Agriculture for the other provinces. I think the Federal Government should invite the co-operation of the various Provincial Governments, and that a united demand should go from Canada insisting on the removal of this embargo. If that were done I think there would be a greater chance of the embargo being lifted and thus removing an injustice which has existed for so many years. The Prime Minister said it seemed to him, and I must admit the same idea has occurred to me, that the embargo is retained more as a protective measure than as a safeguard against the introduction of disease. My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) and my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) have proved to our entire satisfaction that the disease complained of does not exist 'among Canadian herds. Under all the circumstances if the embargo is removed I will accord a certain amount of credit to the Federal Government, and I would be ready likewise to give credit to some of the Provincial Governments.
Sub-amendment agreed to, and motion as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Resuming the adjourned debate on the motion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) for the second reading of Bill No. 17, to define Canadian nationals, adjourned from March 8.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that this debate was adjourned by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McM-aster).

I merely adjourned the debate, Mr. Speaker, for the purpose of getting over an impasse, and not with any intention of contributing to it until I had listened with the same attention as I always do to the extensive remarks
The more extensive remarks.

-to the more extensive remarks of the right hon. Minister of Justice.
Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I beg to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that this Bill is a reprint of the original Bill as proposed to be amended in Committee of the whole House. Mr. Doherty moves to amend clause one by striking out all the words after the word "persons" in the first line and substituting the following words:
-shall be deemed to be Canadian nationals, viz:-	.
(a)	Any British subject who is a Canadian citizen within the meaning of the Immigration Act, Chapter 27 of the Statutes of 1910, as heretofore amended.
(b)	The wife of any such citizen.
(c)	Any person born out of Canada whose father was a Canadian national at the time of that person's birth.
Shall the amendment carry?

May I call the attention of the committee to the French version of the Bill? If I understood the explanation of the Minister of Justice, this "Canadian national" was originally baptized in French at the League of Nations, and then was translated into English. I see that the English version was first used before this House and then translated into French, and that translation does not correspond with the original term which was born at the League of Nations. Of course, this is a matter that cannot very well be left to the translators, as, if so, it generally brings confusion later on. In order that the English version which I have in my hand should correspond with the French version, I would first ask the Minister of Justice if he would not consider it advisable that section one instead of reading "The following persons shall be deemed to be," should read, "The following persons shall be Canadian nationals"? For, after all, we make them Canadian nationals, and we do not want to have anything equivocal about their status. Therefore in the latter form it would correspond with the French version, "Sont reputees ressortissantes du Canada les personnes suivantes, savoir."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would have no objection to accepting the modification. I may explain that instead of declaring that certain persons are British subjects, or that certain persons are Canadian nationals -which, I am prepared to admit, seems to be the more natural and more direct expression-it seems for a very long time past to have been the practice to say that certain persons "shall be deemed to be" etc. In the draft as it was originally before the Jlouse the words "the following persons are Canadian nationals" were used. I see no objection to accepting the definition, if the hon. gentleman thinks it is important. I believe the meaning is absolutely the same. But if we are going to modify it, I would rather say "the following persons are Canadian nationals," than "the following persons shall be Canadians nationals."
That is better.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg therefore to move that section one, as now before the committee, be amended by substituting the word "are" for the words "shall be deemed to be."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Doherty moves to amend section one, as proposed to be amended, by striking out the words "shall
[The Chairman.]
be deemed to be" and replacing them by the word "are." Shall the sub-amendment carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think we might just as well deal with the French version at the same time.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I beg to move to amend subsection one in the French version by substituting the words "sont ressortissantes" for the words "sont reputees ressortissantes."
M. le PRESIDENT: M. Doherty propose que la premiere clause du Bill 17, version frangaise, spit amendee en remplagant les mots "sont reputees ressortissantes" par les mots "sont ressortissantes."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg to further amend that same section by striking out the words "les personnes suivantes, savoir:" so the section would read: "Sont ressortissants du Canada."

Is there such a thing now as a Canadian national? Is it right to say, "the following persons are Canadian nationals," or do we not by this Bill make them so? It is a very fine distinction ; I merely call the hon. gentleman's attention to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that both
things are true. There does exist to-day such a thing as a Canadian national; if there does not, then all those who are proud of the fact that they are Canadians have been attaching to themselves a designation that means nothing. It is equally true that this Act, speaking the day it is passed, declares the fact to exist that certain persons are Canadian nationals. The moment this Bill is passed-whether by virtue of this law or by virtue of any anterior thing is immaterial-these people are Canadian nationals.

The present tense is used in the expectation that the Bill will pass. If the Bill does not pass, then anything provided in it is of no avail. I take it, therefore, looking at the matter from the purely legal aspect, that it is correct to use the present tense.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is quite right. The Bill speaks the moment it is passed; until that moment it says nothing.

If there is no such thing as a Canadian national, how can it be said, as set forth in subsection (c) of sec-

tion 1, that any person born out of Canada "whose father was a Canadian national at the time of that person's birth," shall be a Canadian national?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that the verb "was" as used there has in mind the fact that we are speaking of a person who will be born in the future. The reference is to any person whose father "was" a Canadian national when that person was born.
But there is no such thing as a Canadian national.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman does not suppose there are going to be no children born in the future; that our Canadian nationals are all going to be barren?
Some of them are barons.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: But not barren. I am really puzzled to know how to make it any clearer. Perhaps my hon. friend will suggest a method.
Prior to the introduction of this Bill was there any correspondence on the subject between the Canadian Government and the British Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

I understand that this Bill is a very important one in that it gives to Canadian citizens what might be called a separate status from that of a British subject. Has the Government in any way, shape or form conferred with the British authorities, formally or informally, with regard to this measure?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. The hon. gentleman is under a misapprehension if he thinks that this Bill modifies to the extent of one iota the status of any of us as British subjects. It did not seem to the Government necessary to ask the permission of the British Government-which, I am sure, would not have had the slightest objection-how we ought to define a Canadian, still leaving that Canadian as a British subject just where he was before. I do not see how the hon. gentleman could regard that as necessary.

Will
this Bill involve any change in the classification of the census returns?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know that there has been in the past any heading in the census returns specifying people as being or not being Canadian nationals.
But do we specify Canadians now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have not the census returns before me, but I am under the impression that people are classified according to the origin of their ancestors. I am not quite certain whether there is a column which classifies people as Canadians.	.
Then it is high time we had some definition of that kind. In our documents we do not recognize a man as a Canadian; he is distributed here and there and all over.
That is for election purposes.

Perhaps so; I have nothing to say on that. But our statutes, our documents and our official returns seem to go out of the way to avoid defining a Canadian. I had thought that this was the beginning of legislation in that direction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I hope it is.

I hope we shall soon have legislation of that kind so that it will be established here, in our documents and otherwise, as well as among all other nations, that there is such a thing as a Canadian. I do not ask for any amendment just now in that direction, but I hope that the Minister of Justice and the Government generally will do what they can to see that a Canadian is at least .recognized on his own statute book; for he has not been so recognized in the past. When I say that I speak for the people of all the provinces. A recognition in our statutes, public documents, etc., of what a Canadian is, would be a further step towards the unification of the people of this country.

I endorse the view of my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean). It is because I think it is a step in that direction that I heartily support the Bill. I was sorry I was not here when the second reading was moved.

The Minister spoke
about trying to make clear subsection (t' of section 1, which provides that any person, born out of Canada "whose father was a Canadian national at the time of that person's birth" shall be deemed to be a Canadian national. That language imports the idea that there was such a thing as a Canadian national prior to the passing of this Bill. I take it from the minister that there is no such thing until this Bill is passed, so that a boy or girl born ten years



ago or five days ago could not say that his or her father was a Canadian national at the time of that child's birth, because there was no such thing then. If this is intended to apply after the Bill is passed and assented to, I see two things. The provision that "Any person born out of Canada whose father is a Canadian national at the time of that person's birth," will apply to the future; it does not cover the past. Therefore, the clause is worthy of a little consideration, when we are taking what I conceive to be a rather important step in defining Canadian nationality. I quite agree with the remarks of the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) and the hon. member for East Quebec (Mr. Lapointe), in their desire, which I apprehend is the desire of the whole House, so to define Canadian nationality that it will appear in everything Canadian from this time forward.

I am not a lawyer, but I say that the original draft of the Bill was more to the point and to the argument we are now making, that is, if the words "shall be deemed to be" are in the Bill. I have seen in the Statutes, especially in past practice, a good many clauses where that term is constantly used. If we are creating a new thing and making a new departure here to-day, beginning to establish and recognize at this late hour a Canadian national, the most emphatic way of asserting it is to put in those Vfery words: "shall be deemed to be." I will not press that for the moment on the Minister of Justice; but'I think, when he consults his law officers and the practice heretofore in our statute books, he will find that the term "shall be deemed to be" as it was first read in this chamber this evening, is not only more explicit, but announces the beginning of a new condition of affairs, and we are now beginning to define what a Canadian national is. It will be another landmark in the creation of Canadian nationality.

I do not think the Minister of Justice has quite caught the point raised by the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy). Let me state a case. Twenty years ago a British subject residing in Ontario moved his family across to the United States, and a year later a son was born to them. That son to-day is nineteen years of age. Does he become a Canadian national under this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
The minister thinks he does.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am quite sure.

The clause reads:
Any person born out of Canada whose father was a Canadian national at the time of that person's birth.
That person was born nineteen years ago. The hon. member for North Perth says-and I agree with him there-that there was then no such thing as a Canadian national, and, therefore, that does not bring the son nineteen years of age today and residing in Buffalo, within this Bill.
Does my hon. friend contend that the original drafting would convey the intention he wishes to see conveyed?

I rather thought the expression "shall be deemed to be" was a better one, but that was objected to, and apparently with good reasons. My objection goes to the root of the whole business. I think it is nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I rose hoping to be in agreement with my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) , but unfortunately his last statement makes that impossible. I am disposed to think, as suggested by the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy), that the definition as it is in the Bill, is not wide enough to cover a person born before the passing of this measure, but I think we can find a form of words that will produce that result by letting the present clause stand as it is, but by adding to it in this way.
(c)	Any person born out of Canada whose father was a Canadian national at the time of that person's birth, or with regard to a person born before the passing of this Act whose father at the time of such person's birth possessed all the qualifications of a Canadian national as defined in this Act.
I think that will make the matter clear.

I am not a lawyer like
most of the gentlemen who have spoken on the Bill, and I realize that perhaps I am rather bold in attempting to point out what seems to me to be a lack of consistency between subsection (a) of section 1 on the one hand and subsections (b) and (c). Subsection (a) reads:
The following persons shall be deemed to be Canadian nationals, viz :-(a) any British subject who is a Canadian citizen within the meaning of the Immigration Act, chapter 27 of the Statutes of 1910, as heretofore amended.
In looking up the Immigration Act, chapter 27, section 2, I find the last paragraph of subsection (f) reads:

Provided that for the purpose of this Act a woman who has not been landed in Canada shall not be held to have acquired Canadian citizenship by virtue of her husband being a Canadian citizen; neither shall a child, who has not been landed in Canada be held to have acquired Canadian citizenship through its father or mother being a Canadian citizen.
That seems to exclude certain women and certain men, and yet subsection (b) of the Bill states specifically that the wife of any such citizen shall be deemed to be a Canadian national, and subsection (c) reads:
Any person born out of Canada whose father was a Canadian national at the time of that person's birth.	.
There is an inconsistency there. If we interpret according to subsection (a) and the Immigration Act, certain women and certain men would not be included, and yet subsection (b) makes no exception whatever; it says simply "the wife of any such citizen." I do not know whether the point is well taken or not. '

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are here defining
Canadian nationals. The Immigration Act was defining a Canadian citizen. The first subsection in this Bill makes everybody who is a Canadian citizen a Canadian national, and the two other subsections deal with people who are not necessarily Canadian citizens. With regard to the wife, it seemed to us proper that the wife of a Canadian national should be a Canadian national. In the Immigration Act there is a special and particular reason for not recognizing necessarily as a Canadian citizen the wife of a person who is a Canadian citizen, and the purpose of making a distinction there was to prevent a woman who never had been in Canada, and who perhaps might be subject to some objection from the immigration point of view, from coming into Canada merely because her husband had succeeded in meeting all the requirements and had become a Canadian citizen. The Immigration Act is dealing with immigration, and the term "Canadian citizen" has in that Act a meaning only with regard to immigration. We have, however, taken everybody who is a Canadian citizen under that Act and recognized him or her as a Canadian national, because that Act put upon the definition of a Canadian citizen every restriction that was thought necessary with regard to people coming into this country. If in the Immigration Act the wife of a Canadian citizen as such, without any other condition, had become a Canadian citizen we need not have said anything about her in this Act; but we are doing so because we
do not see the necessity of maintaining with regard to a Canadian national the same distinction which from the immigration point of view it was thought desirable to make in the case of a person who never was in Canada.
With regard to the Canadian citizen suppose a man came into this country and acquired Canadian citizenship under the Immigration Act and then went out and married the most notorious prostitute, a woman of the worst of habits. It would not -be thought desirable, would it, that because she had married that Canadian- citizen, she should be entitled to come right into our country? She will not be entitled to come right into our country and therefore in this Act it does not seem necessary to make the same distinction with regard to a Canadian national. Though under this Act she may be entitled to call herself a Canadian national, under the Immigration Act she would not be entitled to come into Canada,

In view of the point raised by my hon. friend from North Waterloo, and the explanation given by the Minister of Justice, may I suggest to him that a good deal of confusion with regard to the interpretation of this section might be avoided if no part of that interpretation was dependent upon the language of some other statute? If, instead of this reference in subsection (a) to another Act, a definition were given in the subsection without reference to any other Act, there would be less danger of confusion, because the other Act upon which the interpretation of this subsection depends may be amended from time to time, and consequently the definition in this Act will be affected by such amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member will notice that in referring to the definition we refer to "a Canadian citizen within the meaning of The Immigration Act, chapter twenty-seven of the statutes of 1910, as heretofore amended." We say, "as heretofore amended." We are fixing it now. It is not going to follow that because somebody amends the Immigration Act in the future, that that amendment will affect this Act:
With regard to the other part of it, what seemed to us was this: We get a definition in the Immigration Act as it stands that is satisfactory. What would be gained by copying that definition into this statute? I think that there is some value in connecting your legislation, but all that we were concerned with in this Act,

once we had come to the conclusion that the definition of a Canadian citizen in the Immigration Act was satisfactory as far as it went, was to provide for people, if there were any, who we thought ought to be Canadian nationals, though they did not come within the definition of a Canadian citizen as contained in the Immigration Act, and those two classes are the people dealt with in (b) and (c). The Immigration Act, peculiarly enough, does not say anywhere that the wife of a Canadian citizen, even after she has come *in o Canada, and is accepted, is by the fact *x her being the wife of a Canadian citizen, a Canadian citizen herself, but it does enact as though it thought that if she were landed in Canada the mere fact that her husband was a Canadian citizen would make her one. It does enact negativing her right to be a Canadian citizen merely because her husband is one, unless she has been landed in Canada. That, I think, is a very wise provision from the point of view of immigration. It protects us from the coming in of improper people merely because they happen to be the wives of perfectly proper people perhaps. It did not seem to us in dealing with the definition of a Canadian national generally, where there was no question of the country being practically affected, that it was necessary to get down to as fine a definition as that. We thought we might safely follow what is a general rule in all legislation I have seen with regard to nationality, namely, that the wife of the man has the nationality he has.
I quite understand that it is possible for a person to be a Canadian national, and yet not be a Canadian citizen, but it seemed to me there was some conflict in the various subsections.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is an intentional difference.
Is it .fair to assume, then, that sub-sections (b) and (c) are inserted in order to over-ride the disqualification that would otherwise exist by virtue of subsection (a) of the Immigration Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. The Immigration Act stands absolutely untouched, and as regards immigration will continue absolutely to govern.
